course.title: Data Engineering: Pipelines, Warehouses and Lakehouses
course.description: How data moves from sources to analysis: pipelines, file and table formats, warehouses and lakehouses, batch and streaming processing, and running it all reliably.
course.audience: A capable adult who can query a table with SQL and read short Python programs (sql-from-rows-to-reports and python-for-data-analysis), preparing for work as a data engineer or for a certification such as Microsoft DP-700. No previous platform experience is assumed; named products are examples only.

paragraphs: Most of the figures that people analyse, such as a day's revenue or the number of customers who ordered last week, were never read directly from the system that produced them. The rows were copied out of an orders database or an event stream, cleaned, joined to other data and written to a table built for reading, usually by a chain of scheduled jobs that nobody looks at until a figure is wrong. Data engineering is the work of building those chains so that the table at the end can be trusted, which is harder than it sounds, because every job will at some point fail and be run again, and every source will at some point send a row late, twice or in a shape nobody expected.

Much of the subject can be settled with arithmetic before anything runs. Whether a rerun doubles a table follows from how its rows are written, the bytes a query reads follow from how the files are laid out and which of them a filter can skip, and the time a job takes follows from the number of its tasks, the cores they share and the size of its largest key. Products such as Microsoft Fabric, Spark, Delta Lake and Iceberg appear as examples, and the same reasoning holds on whichever platform you use, so that you can predict what a pipeline will do and find the cause when it does something else.
outcomes: You'll be able to design a pipeline as a graph and make each step safe to rerun.
You'll be able to compare file formats, table formats and architectures by what a query must read.
You'll be able to work through partitions, shuffles, windows and watermarks with numbers.
You'll be able to decide how to check, monitor, secure and release a data pipeline.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on SQL: From Rows to Reports, Python for Data Analysis.

modules.title: Moving data
modules.description: What a pipeline is, the formats it carries, loading without duplicates, capturing changes and running the steps in order.

modules.title: Storing data
modules.description: Warehouses, lakes and lakehouses, the open table formats that make files behave like tables, and how layout decides what a query reads.

modules.title: Processing data
modules.description: Distributed batch processing, cleaning and deduplicating, and streaming with event time and watermarks.

modules.title: Running data platforms
modules.description: Checking data as it moves, watching pipelines in production, and promoting and securing them across environments.

concepts.title: Pipeline
concepts.summary: A pipeline is a set of steps that moves data from sources to a destination, with each step reading the output of the one before.

concepts.title: Batch and streaming
concepts.summary: Batch processes a bounded set of data on a schedule, while streaming processes an unbounded flow record by record or in small groups.

concepts.title: ETL and ELT
concepts.summary: ETL transforms data before loading it, ELT loads raw data first and transforms it inside the destination.

concepts.title: Idempotence
concepts.summary: A step is idempotent when running it twice leaves the destination in the same state as running it once.

concepts.title: Row and column layout
concepts.summary: A row format stores each record together, while a columnar format stores each column together, which suits queries that read few columns of many rows.

concepts.title: Parquet structure
concepts.summary: A Parquet file holds row groups, each with a column chunk per column, and a footer with the schema and per-chunk statistics.

concepts.title: Encoding and compression
concepts.summary: Similar values stored together compress well, so a column of repeated values shrinks far more than the same values scattered across rows.

concepts.title: Schema in the file
concepts.summary: CSV carries no types and JSON carries names but not a fixed schema, while Parquet records column names and types in its footer.

concepts.title: Full and incremental loads
concepts.summary: A full load replaces the destination from the whole source, while an incremental load moves only rows that changed since the last run.

concepts.title: Watermark
concepts.summary: A stored high-water mark, such as the latest updated_at already loaded, marks where the next incremental run starts.

concepts.title: Upsert (merge)
concepts.summary: An upsert updates the row when its key exists and inserts it when it does not, so replaying a batch changes nothing.

concepts.title: Late-arriving rows
concepts.summary: A row committed at the source after the watermark has moved past its timestamp is skipped by a strict greater-than filter.

concepts.title: Change data capture
concepts.summary: CDC reads the source's change record, with an operation and a position for each insert, update and delete, instead of repeatedly querying the table.

concepts.title: Order by log position
concepts.summary: Changes must be applied in log order, because an update arriving before the insert it follows would be lost or misplaced.

concepts.title: Deletes
concepts.summary: A timestamp query cannot see a row that has gone, so deletes need the log, a soft-delete flag or a periodic key comparison.

concepts.title: Replicated copies
concepts.summary: A mirrored or replicated copy applies the log to keep a read-only analytic copy near-current without custom code.

concepts.title: Directed acyclic graph
concepts.summary: Tasks are nodes and dependencies are arrows with no cycles, so there is always an order in which every task runs after its inputs.

concepts.title: Critical path
concepts.summary: The longest chain of dependent task durations sets the minimum time to finish, however many tasks run in parallel.

concepts.title: Retries and backoff
concepts.summary: A failed task is retried a limited number of times with growing waits, which only helps if the task is idempotent.

concepts.title: Backfill
concepts.summary: Re-running a pipeline for past periods works by giving each run its own period as a parameter, in parallel up to a limit.

concepts.title: Warehouse
concepts.summary: A warehouse stores structured, modelled data under a schema it enforces on write, and serves SQL analytics with strong consistency.

concepts.title: Data lake
concepts.summary: A lake keeps files of any kind in cheap object storage with structure applied when they are read.

concepts.title: Lakehouse
concepts.summary: A lakehouse puts a table format and transactions over lake files so one copy serves both engineering and SQL analytics.

concepts.title: Medallion layers
concepts.summary: Bronze holds data as received, silver holds cleaned and conformed data, and gold holds business-ready aggregates.

concepts.title: Transaction log
concepts.summary: A table format records each commit as a list of files added and removed, and a table is the set of files not yet removed at a chosen version.

concepts.title: Snapshots and atomic commit
concepts.summary: A commit becomes visible all at once, so a reader sees a complete earlier version or a complete later one, never half of a write.

concepts.title: Time travel
concepts.summary: Because old versions are recorded, a query can read the table as of a version or time until the old files are removed.

concepts.title: Compaction and vacuum
concepts.summary: Compaction rewrites many small files into fewer large ones, and vacuum deletes files no longer referenced after a retention period.

concepts.title: Partition pruning
concepts.summary: When data is split into directories by a column, a filter on that column lets the engine skip every other directory.

concepts.title: Partition cardinality
concepts.summary: A partition column needs a modest number of distinct values, because tens of thousands of tiny partitions cost more to list than they save.

concepts.title: Small files
concepts.summary: Many small files add per-file overhead for listing, opening and metadata, so writers target files of hundreds of megabytes.

concepts.title: Data skipping
concepts.summary: Per-file minimum and maximum statistics let an engine skip files whose range cannot match a filter, and clustering sorts data so the ranges are tight.

concepts.title: Partitions and tasks
concepts.summary: A distributed engine splits data into partitions and runs one task per partition, in waves limited by the number of cores.

concepts.title: Narrow and wide transformations
concepts.summary: Narrow steps such as filter and map work within each partition, while wide steps such as group by and join move rows between partitions in a shuffle.

concepts.title: Lazy evaluation
concepts.summary: Transformations only build a plan, and an action such as count or write triggers the work, which lets the engine optimise the plan first.

concepts.title: Skew and broadcast
concepts.summary: A key holding most of the rows makes one task far slower than the rest, and joining a small table can avoid a shuffle by sending it to every executor.

concepts.title: Keep the latest per key
concepts.summary: ROW_NUMBER over a partition by the key, ordered by load time descending, then keeping row 1, removes duplicates and keeps the newest record.

concepts.title: Typing and trimming
concepts.summary: Raw text is trimmed and cast to its true type in the silver step, and values that cannot be cast become explicit nulls or rejects.

concepts.title: Order of steps
concepts.summary: Deduplicate before aggregating, because a sum over duplicated rows counts the same event more than once.

concepts.title: Rejects
concepts.summary: Rows that fail typing go to a rejects table with the reason, so nothing disappears silently.

concepts.title: Event time and processing time
concepts.summary: Event time is when something happened, processing time is when the system saw it, and the gap between them is lateness.

concepts.title: Windows
concepts.summary: A tumbling window is fixed and non-overlapping, a sliding window overlaps when its slide is shorter than its length, and a session window closes after a gap with no events.

concepts.title: Watermark
concepts.summary: The watermark is the maximum event time seen minus the allowed lateness, and windows ending before it are finalised and their state dropped.

concepts.title: Delivery guarantees
concepts.summary: With at-least-once delivery a failure replays records, so a sink that is idempotent or deduplicates by key makes the result effectively exactly once.

concepts.title: Validation gate
concepts.summary: A gate checks schema, ranges and keys at a layer boundary and decides to pass, quarantine or stop the run.

concepts.title: Schema evolution
concepts.summary: Adding a nullable column is usually safe, while removing, renaming or retyping a column breaks readers.

concepts.title: Quarantine and dead letters
concepts.summary: Failing rows are written aside with the reason, so good rows continue and bad rows can be fixed and replayed.

concepts.title: Fail fast on drift
concepts.summary: If a source changes shape unexpectedly, stopping the run loudly is better than loading wrong data quietly.

concepts.title: Freshness
concepts.summary: Freshness is the age of the newest data in a table, checked against a target such as under six hours.

concepts.title: Throughput and latency
concepts.summary: Throughput is rows or bytes per second, and latency is the time from arrival to availability.

concepts.title: Run signals
concepts.summary: Duration, rows in and out, retries and failures per run reveal problems before users do.

concepts.title: Common slow causes
concepts.summary: Skew, too many small files, unneeded shuffles, reading unneeded columns and under-sized capacity cause most slow jobs.

concepts.title: Environments
concepts.summary: Development, test and production are separate places with the same structure, and a release promotes tested changes rather than editing production.

concepts.title: Version control and deployment
concepts.summary: Pipeline definitions live in a repository, and an automated deployment applies them to each environment with environment-specific parameters.

concepts.title: Access control
concepts.summary: Roles grant access to workspaces and items, and finer controls restrict rows, columns or files to the people who need them.

concepts.title: Secrets and identities
concepts.summary: Credentials are held in a secret store and used by service identities, never written into code or notebooks.

lessons.title: What a pipeline is

lead.text: In the figure, data enters at two **sources**, the orders database and the product list, which are the places where the data already lives. The first step lands a raw copy of the orders somewhere the pipeline controls, so that the later steps are not reading from a database that people are still typing into. The clean step then removes the test orders, the join attaches each order's price from the product list, and the total step adds the revenue up by hour. The table the dashboard reads is the **sink**, the place where the pipeline's result is written.

Every arrow means that the next step reads what the previous one wrote, so the chain forms a graph in which a step can start only when everything it reads has finished. The join has two arrows pointing into it, which means it waits for both the clean step and the product list, whereas the land step waits for nothing else. Drawing a pipeline as a graph is therefore more than a convention, because the graph holds exactly the information a scheduler needs to decide what can run and what must wait.

afterFigure.text: Switch the figure to the row counts and follow the numbers: 1,200 orders become 1,180 once the clean step has dropped 20 test orders, the join keeps all 1,180 because each order matches one product, and the total step reduces them to 24 rows, one for each hour of the day.

diagram.alt: A directed graph of an orders pipeline. The orders source feeds a land step, then a clean step. The clean step and a product list both feed a join, which feeds an hourly total, which writes the dashboard table.
diagram.caption: Each arrow means the next step reads what the one before it wrote. Use the buttons to see the row counts.

reveal.text: A join pairs each order with its product, so its output is as long as the list of orders, not as long as the two inputs put together.

lead.text: The same orders can be processed in two quite different rhythms. In **batch** processing the pipeline waits until a fixed set of data has collected, such as all of yesterday's orders, and then runs over that set in one go. The set has a beginning and an end, which is what it means for the data to be *bounded*, and a nightly copy of orders or a weekly report is batch work. In **streaming** the data is treated as a flow with no end, and each record, or each small group of records, is processed within moments of arriving.

Between the two sits **micro-batch**, which runs a very small batch every few seconds or minutes and so behaves like a stream at a coarser grain. The figure shows eight orders under the three rhythms, and the two things worth comparing are when the first order is counted and how many runs the pipeline needs.

afterFigure.text: It is tempting to describe streaming as batch made faster, but speed is the smaller difference. A stream never ends, so there is never a moment at which all the data has arrived. Records can arrive out of order, because a phone that was offline sends its sale late, and a result computed from a stream is a figure that keeps being *updated* instead of a figure that is finished. A later lesson takes up each of these problems.

diagram.alt: Eight orders on a time line handled three ways. Batch gathers them into one run at 02:00. Micro-batch runs three short batches. Streaming handles each order as it arrives.
diagram.caption: Compare when the first order is counted and how many runs happen. Use the buttons to switch rhythm.

reveal.text: The data the job reads has a start and an end, and the job runs on a schedule, which is the mark of batch work.

lead.text: The clean step has to run somewhere, and where it runs gives two orderings of the same three actions. In **ETL**, short for extract, transform, load, the pipeline reads the data from the source, cleans it in a separate engine, and loads only the cleaned result into the destination. In **ELT** the pipeline extracts the data and loads it as it is, then transforms it inside the destination with the destination's own engine, usually in SQL.

The figure uses 1,000 raw rows of which 40 are unusable. With ETL the destination receives only the 960 good rows, so the raw copy exists nowhere except at the source. With ELT the destination holds all 1,000 in a raw table and the 960 in a cleaned table beside it.

afterFigure.text: ELT does not mean that the data is never transformed, which is a common misreading of the name. The cleaning still happens, and what changes is where the code runs and what is kept. Keeping the raw rows means that a mistake in the cleaning logic can be repaired by running it again over the original data, which is why many pipelines on a **lakehouse**, a store of open data files that can be queried like a warehouse, land raw files first and clean them afterwards. ETL remains a sensible choice when the destination must never hold sensitive raw fields.

reveal.text: The cleaned rows go into a second table, so the raw table is left as it was loaded.
A plain `INSERT` has no memory of earlier runs, so the table holds six rows, three of them copies. The next screen gives the missing property a name.

lead.text: The plain insert from the previous screen leaves 6 rows, and the figure shows the fault that makes reruns dangerous. The step did exactly what it was told each time, but the second run added a second copy of every row, so any total built on the table is now doubled. A step that avoids this is called **idempotent**: running it twice leaves the destination in the same state as running it once.

There are two common ways to get that property. An **upsert** writes each row under a key, replacing the row that has the same key or adding the row if there is none, so a second run finds all its rows already present and changes nothing. An **overwrite** deletes the slice of the destination that the run is responsible for, such as one day, and writes the slice again, so the second run replaces what the first one wrote.

afterFigure.text: Idempotence matters because production pipelines run again and again. A failed night is retried, a late file triggers a repeat, and a fix to the logic is applied to history by running old dates a second time. A scheduler can retry a step safely only when the step has this property, which is why the later lesson on orchestration depends on it.

steps.headline: Load a batch of orders 10, 11, 12 and 13 into a table that already holds 10 and 11, using an upsert on order_id, and run it twice.

workedSteps.text: Before the first run the table holds two rows.
The first run finds that ids 10 and 11 exist and replaces those rows, and it adds ids 12 and 13 because they are new.
The second run finds all four ids present, so it replaces them with identical rows and adds nothing. Work out how many rows the table holds now.

reveal.text: Each run first removes the day's rows and then writes them again, so the retry replaces the three rows and the table ends at 10 rows. Overwriting a slice is idempotent for the same reason an upsert is.

lessons.orientation: Follow orders through a pipeline, tell batch from streaming and ETL from ELT, and see why a rerun has to be safe.
lessons.nextAction: Compare row-based and column-based file formats by the bytes a query has to read.

blocks.text: A shop's orders database records every sale as a row holding an order id, a product, a quantity and the time it was placed. The sales dashboard on the manager's screen shows revenue for each hour of the day, and nothing in the orders table can answer that directly, because it holds single orders and not totals. Something has to copy the rows out, remove the test orders that staff have typed in, attach each product's price and add everything up by hour, and that chain of steps, with raw data entering at one end and a finished table leaving at the other, is a **data pipeline**.

What makes it more than a script is that it does not run once. The dashboard has to be fresh again tomorrow, a step will fail on some night and be run again, and a mistake found in March means that three months of results have to be worked out afresh. A pipeline is something that runs repeatedly, so the question of what happens when a step runs twice matters as much as the question of what the step does.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to classify a workload as batch or streaming, choose between ETL and ELT, and spot a step that is not safe to rerun.
intro.whyItMatters: Almost every later lesson, from loading to scheduling, assumes a pipeline drawn as a graph and steps that can be rerun safely.

recap.keyIdea: A pipeline carries data from sources through steps to a sink, and because it will be rerun, each step has to be idempotent.

blocks.text: You followed 1,200 orders through steps that each read what the one before had written, and saw that the same flow can run as a nightly batch, as micro-batches or as a stream, and can clean its data before loading it (ETL) or after (ELT). The step that mattered most was the one run twice: a plain insert turned 3 rows into 6, while an upsert or an overwrite of the day left the table as it was.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at the files these steps read and write, and at how the layout of a file decides how many bytes a query has to read.

lessons.title: Files and formats

lead.text: A table has two natural shapes on disk. Written one record after another, which is how a CSV file or a database row store keeps it, the four values of the first order sit together and are followed by the four values of the second. Written one column after another, the six order ids come first, then the six customer names, then the six amounts, and so on. A layout of the first kind is called **row-oriented** and a layout of the second kind is called **columnar**.

The difference shows when a query needs only some of the columns. The query in the figure adds up amt for each country, so it needs two of the four columns. Suppose every value takes 8 bytes. A reader of the row layout has to pass over all 24 values, which is 192 bytes, because the amounts and the countries are scattered between the other values. A reader of the column layout goes straight to the two blocks it needs and reads 12 values, which is 96 bytes.

afterFigure.text: The saving is the fraction of the columns the query needs: two columns of four means half the bytes, and two columns of twenty means a tenth. A wide analytical table, with dozens of columns and queries that touch a handful, is where a columnar layout pays off most.

diagram.alt: A table of six orders with four columns, id, cust, amt and ctry, drawn as 24 cells in storage order. In the row layout the cells for amt and ctry are scattered across the strip and the reader passes over all 192 bytes. In the column layout they form two blocks and the reader fetches 96 bytes.

reveal.text: Only the needed columns are read, and each is 50,000,000 values of 8 bytes, so 1,200,000,000 bytes or 1.2 GB.
Only the third range contains 600, so one group is read and three are skipped. The next screen shows where those ranges are kept.

lead.text: Parquet is the best-known columnar format, and it does not store each column as one enormous block. It cuts the table into **row groups**, each holding a block of consecutive rows, and inside a row group every column is stored on its own as a **column chunk**. The file ends with a **footer** that holds the schema, which is the column names and types, and for each column chunk a few statistics, among them the smallest and the largest value in it.

A reader opens a Parquet file at its end, reads the footer, and only then decides which chunks to fetch. The statistics are what let it skip work: a row group whose `order_id` range is 1 to 200 cannot contain `order_id` 450, so a filter on 450 does not need to read it at all. The figure shows the layout and then two filters over five row groups.

afterFigure.text: A skip is possible only when the ranges are informative. If the rows were written in no particular order, every group could span almost the whole range of order ids, and no group could be ruled out. Skipping works best on a column that the file happens to be ordered by.

reveal.text: Both 100 to 260 and 240 to 400 include 250, so two groups are read. The overlap is what weakens the skipping.

lead.text: Keeping a column's values together has a second benefit. A column holds values of one kind, and often many that repeat: a country column with three distinct values across a million rows can be stored as the three names and a short code for each row, a scheme called **dictionary encoding**, and ordinary compression then shrinks the codes further. The same values scattered between columns of other kinds have neighbours that differ, and they compress far less.

Formats also differ in what they say about the data. A CSV file carries no types at all, so the text 04/03/2026 is 4 March for one reader and 3 April for another, and a value that contains a comma has to be wrapped in quotes that every reader must handle the same way. JSON lines names each field but has no fixed schema, so one line may hold a string where the line before held a number. Parquet and Avro both record the schema with the data, so a reader gets the column names and types from the file itself.

afterFigure.text: Avro writes its data row by row, with the schema in the file's header, which suits messages that are produced and consumed one record at a time. The table sets the four formats side by side.

steps.headline: A table has 200,000,000 rows and 12 columns of 4 bytes. A query needs 3 of the columns. Compare the bytes read under the two layouts.

workedSteps.text: A row-oriented reader passes over every column of every row.
A columnar reader fetches only the 3 columns the query needs, each of 200,000,000 values of 4 bytes.
The columnar layout reads 3 of the 12 columns, a quarter of the bytes.

lead.text: Columnar layout is a bet that queries read a few columns of many rows. A job that does the opposite loses by it: to fetch one complete order by its key, a row layout reads one contiguous run of bytes, whereas a column layout has to visit a separate place for each column and then put the record back together. A service that looks up single records thousands of times a second is therefore better served by a row layout.

The four formats of the table fit four common jobs. CSV is read by people and spreadsheets and is acceptable for small exports and for handing data to another organisation, as long as its lack of types is managed. JSON lines suits logs and events whose fields vary. Avro suits messages sent one record at a time, where each record is complete in itself. Parquet suits the repeated analytical queries that make up most of a warehouse's work, and it is the format that the later lessons on table formats and partitioning build on.

reveal.text: The record's values sit together in a row layout, so one contiguous read returns the whole order.
Raw bytes for the 4 columns are 320 MB, and a quarter of that is 80 MB. Column choice and compression multiply together, which is why a columnar file can read a small share of the table's raw size.

lessons.orientation: Compare row and column layouts by the bytes a query must read, and see what a Parquet footer lets a reader skip.
lessons.nextAction: Choose between a full and an incremental load, and predict the row count when a load is replayed.

blocks.text: A table of 100 million orders, each with twenty columns of eight bytes, comes to 16 billion bytes when it is written out value by value. A question such as revenue by country needs only two of those columns, and yet whether it reads 16 GB or 1.6 GB is settled by nothing in the question. It depends on how the file was laid out at the time it was written.

That layout is the file format. Written row by row, the twenty values of one order sit together, so a query that wants two of them has to pass over all twenty, while written column by column each column sits in a block of its own and the query can fetch only the two blocks it needs. A format that suits one kind of question makes another kind more expensive, so choosing one is a decision about how the table will be read, and multiplying rows, columns and bytes tells you what each choice will cost before any query runs.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to work out the bytes a query reads under a row and a column layout, read a Parquet footer's statistics to see which row groups are skipped, and pick a format for a job.
intro.whyItMatters: The same table can cost a query 16 GB or 1.6 GB, depending on a choice made when the file was written.

recap.keyIdea: A columnar file lets a query read only the columns it needs, and a Parquet footer lets it skip row groups, so the layout decides how many bytes are read.

blocks.text: You compared the bytes read by a row layout and a column layout for the same query, and found that the columnar reader fetches only the fraction of columns it needs, with compression shrinking that further. Parquet adds row groups and a footer of minimum and maximum values, which let a reader skip whole groups when a filter falls outside their range, though overlapping ranges weaken the effect. Row layouts keep their place for fetching whole records by key and for messages sent one at a time.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson loads data into a table, and it asks how many rows the table holds when a load is run again.

lessons.title: Loading without duplicates

lead.text: The simplest load replaces the destination with a copy of the whole source. This is a **full load**, and its great virtue is that it is safe to repeat: whatever state the destination was in, it ends as a copy of the source. Its cost is that every run moves every row, so a source of 10,000,000 rows costs 10,000,000 rows of transfer each night even when only 25,000 of them changed that day.

An **incremental load** moves only the rows that changed since the previous run. For the same source that is about 25,000 rows, which is 400 times fewer, but it raises two questions that a full load never has to answer: how the job knows which rows changed, and what happens when it runs again over rows it has already moved. The next screens take the second question first, because it is the one that damages data.

diagram.alt: A source table of 10,000,000 rows and a destination. A full load moves all 10,000,000 rows each night. An incremental load moves only the 25,000 rows that changed that day.
diagram.caption: The same source loaded two ways. Use the buttons to compare the rows that move.

reveal.text: A week of increments is 175,000 rows. A full load would have moved 70,000,000 rows over the same week.
The table holds 7 rows: the original 3 plus 2 from each run, with ids 2 and 4 each present twice. The next screen shows how to make the second run harmless.

lead.text: The 7 rows on the previous screen came from a plain `INSERT`, which adds a row whether or not one with the same identity is already there. To make a replay harmless the table needs a **key**, a column such as `id` whose values identify a row, and the write has to say what to do when the key is already present. An **upsert** does exactly that: when no row has the key it inserts one, and when a row has the key it updates that row. In SQLite and PostgreSQL the statement is written `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET ...`

The figure applies both writes to a products table. The incoming batch carries a new price for pad, product 3, and a new product, tape, product 5. Run twice with a plain `INSERT`, the table grows from 4 rows to 8, with pad appearing three times at two different prices. Run twice as an upsert, the table has 5 rows after the first run and still 5 after the second, because the second run finds both keys present and sets the same values again.

afterFigure.text: If a key is declared on the table, a plain `INSERT` of a row that is already present fails on the second run instead of duplicating it. That prevents the doubled data but stops the pipeline at the point where the retry was meant to rescue it, so the upsert remains the better way to write. Overwriting a slice of the table, from the first lesson, is the other idempotent pattern.

queries.label: Before the load
queries.sql: SELECT * FROM products ORDER BY id;

queries.label: INSERT, run twice
Upsert, run twice

reveal.text: Id 2 is updated and id 4 is added, so the table holds 4 rows after the first run, and the second run changes nothing.

lead.text: Most source tables carry an `updated_at` column that is set whenever a row is written, and an incremental job uses it to find what changed. The job stores the largest `updated_at` it has loaded, a stored mark called the **watermark**. The next run asks for rows beyond the watermark, loads them, and moves the watermark up to the largest `updated_at` among the rows it has just read. The watermark is a value taken from the data, and it is not the clock time at which the job ran, because the source's clock and the job's clock differ and a row can commit after the time it is stamped with.

The comparison is a decision as well. With strictly greater than, a row stamped exactly at the watermark is not read again, and with greater than or equal it is. In the figure the watermark is 14:10 and two rows carry that exact time, so the first filter selects the two later rows and the second selects four rows in all.

afterFigure.text: The second filter looks wasteful, but there is a reason for it. Several rows can share a timestamp, and a run may stop after loading only some of them, so a strict filter would never return to the rest. Reading the ties again costs little when the write is an upsert, which absorbs the repeats, and it cannot lose a row. The upsert and the watermark therefore work as a pair.

steps.headline: Run one incremental load with the watermark at 10:05, over source rows updated at 10:03, 10:05, 10:06 and 10:09, using a strict filter.

workedSteps.text: The job reads the stored watermark.
It asks for rows with `updated_at` greater than 10:05. The rows at 10:03 and 10:05 are not later, so the rows at 10:06 and 10:09 are selected.
It upserts those 2 rows into the destination, so a replay would change nothing.
It then stores the largest `updated_at` among the rows it loaded as the new watermark. Say what the watermark becomes.

lead.text: A watermark carries an assumption, that rows reach the source in the order of their timestamps, and the assumption can fail. A transaction that began a little before a run may commit a little after it, so that its row is stamped below a watermark that has already moved on. In the figure a row stamped 05-02 commits after a run that took the watermark to 05-03, and the filter `updated_at > 05-03` never selects it. The row is lost without an error, and nothing in the destination shows that it is missing. This is the **late row** problem.

The usual remedy is to re-read an overlap. The job starts a fixed interval before the watermark, two days in the figure, and relies on the upsert to absorb the rows it already holds. The overlap costs a few repeated rows and buys the late arrivals. How wide it should be depends on how late rows really arrive at that source, and a row later than the overlap is still lost.

diagram.alt: Source rows by day from 05-01 to 05-04. After a run that moved the watermark to 05-03, a row stamped 05-02 commits late. A strict greater-than filter reads only 05-04 and misses it. A two-day overlap starting at 05-01 catches it.
diagram.caption: The red circle is the late row. Use the buttons to see how each filter treats it.

lessons.orientation: Choose between a full and an incremental load, use a watermark and an upsert, and predict the row count after a replay.
lessons.nextAction: Apply an ordered log of changes to a table, and see why a log catches deletes that a timestamp query misses.

blocks.text: A warehouse table of customers is refreshed every night from the shop's database, and two decisions are hidden in that sentence. The first is which rows to carry across, either all of them or only those that changed since the last run. The second is how to write them, because if the scheduler runs the job twice after the first run seemed to time out, the table must not end up holding a second copy of every row.

The two decisions depend on each other. A load that carries only the changed rows has to know where the previous run stopped, and when it cannot be sure it reads some rows a second time, which is harmless only if the way it writes them can absorb a repeat. Settled together, they let you say for any load how many rows it moves each night and how many the table holds after the load has been retried.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to choose between a full and an incremental load, apply a watermark to a set of rows, and predict how many rows a table holds after a load is replayed.
intro.whyItMatters: Most production loads are retried at some point, so a load that cannot survive a replay will eventually corrupt a table.

recap.keyIdea: An incremental load starts from a watermark and writes with an upsert, so replaying a batch or re-reading an overlap leaves the table unchanged.

blocks.text: You compared a full load, which moves every row and is safe to repeat, with an incremental load that moves only the changed rows. A plain `INSERT` turned 3 rows into 7 when the job was retried, whereas an upsert on a key left 4. The watermark, taken from the largest `updated_at` loaded, tells the next run where to begin, and a short overlap with an upsert recovers rows that commit late.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson asks what a timestamp query can never see, a row that has been deleted, and reads the source's own log of changes instead.

lessons.title: Capturing changes

lead.text: The previous lesson found changed rows with a filter on `updated_at`. The filter works because a changed row carries a new timestamp, and it fails for a row that has been removed, because the row is gone and so is its timestamp. In the figure id 2 is hard-deleted at the source. The nightly query returns the rows that still exist, id 2 is not among them, and the warehouse goes on holding a row that no longer exists anywhere else.

A source database keeps a record of every change that it makes to its tables, so that it can recover after a crash and so that copies of it can be kept up to date. Reading that record in place of the table is called **change data capture**, or CDC. Each entry in it carries an **operation**, which is an insert, an update or a delete, the key of the row it affects, the new values, and a **position** that fixes where it falls in the sequence of changes. A delete is simply another entry, and so the log reader sees it.

afterFigure.text: CDC is therefore a way of asking the database for its own account of what happened, and it is not a product. Products implement it, and some of them are named in the last screens of this lesson.

diagram.alt: A source table with ids 1 to 4 where id 2 has been hard-deleted, and a warehouse copy. A polling query on updated_at never sees id 2, so the copy keeps it. A log reader sees a delete entry for id 2 and removes it.

lead.text: A log of changes can be turned into a table by applying its entries one at a time to a target that starts empty. An insert adds a row with its key and values, an update replaces the values of the row with that key, and a delete removes the row with that key. The figure applies a log of four entries, and each view shows the target after one more entry has been applied.

afterFigure.text: Two things are worth noticing. The log is longer than the table it produces, since four entries leave a single row, because later entries overwrite or remove the effect of earlier ones. And what the target holds at any moment is simply the log applied up to a position, which is why the position matters so much, and why a copy kept up to date this way can be stopped and restarted from the last position it applied.

The delete arrives last and removes the row that position 3 had written, so the table is empty. The next screen says what should have been used for the order.

lead.text: The previous screen shows how a correct log becomes a wrong table. The entries were produced in the order 1, 2, 3, and the correct result is the one in which the row was deleted and then inserted again with the value 'b'. Applied in the order 1, 3, 2, the same three entries leave an empty table, because the delete removes a row that, in the log's own order, did not exist yet when the delete happened.

Networks and parallel readers reorder messages, so arrival order cannot be trusted. The **position** in the log is assigned by the source at the moment the change is committed, and a consumer that sorts by position, and does not apply entry 3 until it has applied entry 2, reproduces the source's history exactly. If an entry is missing, the safe action is to wait for it, and applying the entries that did arrive would be a guess.

workedSteps.text: Entries 1 and 2 add two rows.
Entry 3 replaces the value of id 2, and entry 4 removes id 1.
Entry 5 adds id 4 and entry 6 replaces its value. Say what value id 4 holds when the log ends.

lead.text: The log is the most complete record, but it is not always available, and two other ways of finding deletes are common. A **soft delete** does not remove the row. It sets a flag such as `is_deleted` and updates `updated_at`, so a timestamp query sees the change like any other, and the warehouse can drop or hide the row on its side. A **key comparison** reads the full list of keys from the source and from the warehouse, and every key that is in the warehouse and not in the source has been deleted. The comparison reads the whole key column, which is cheaper than reading the whole table but still more than the log asks for.

Several platforms package the log reader. A mirrored or replicated copy, such as the mirroring of a source database into Microsoft Fabric, applies the source's changes continuously and keeps a read-only analytical copy close to current without custom code. This is an example of the idea and not a requirement, because other platforms offer comparable replication under other names, and underneath they all read a position-ordered log.

reveal.text: Ids 3 and 6 are in the warehouse but not in the source, so 2 rows must be deleted.
Updates change rows without adding or removing any, so the count depends on the inserts and deletes alone: 5 − 2 = 3.

lessons.orientation: Apply an ordered change log to a table, and explain why a log sees deletes that a timestamp query cannot.
lessons.nextAction: Read a pipeline as a graph of tasks, and find its valid orders, its critical path and a backfill plan.

blocks.text: A timestamp filter finds a changed row because the change leaves the row behind with a newer timestamp. A row that is deleted leaves nothing behind, so a nightly query on `updated_at` returns the same rows as before and the warehouse goes on holding a customer who left the source weeks ago. Totals built on that copy are wrong in a way that no check of the load would reveal, since every load succeeded.

The source database does know that the row was deleted, because it wrote the fact down in its own log as it happened. A pipeline that reads that log in place of the table sees every insert, update and delete in the order the source committed them, so that applying the entries one by one, in that order, rebuilds the source table exactly, deletes included.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to apply a change log to a table, explain why polling misses deletes, and say why entries must be applied by position.
intro.whyItMatters: Copies of operational databases are only as good as their handling of deletes and of order, and both are failures that go unnoticed.

recap.keyIdea: A change log records inserts, updates and deletes in a fixed order, so applying it by position reproduces the source, including deletes that a timestamp query misses.

blocks.text: You saw a hard delete slip past a query on `updated_at`, and then replayed logs against empty tables, tracking each key to its last entry. Applied by position the entries reproduce the source, and applied by arrival time they can delete a row that should exist. Soft-delete flags and key comparisons are lighter ways to see deletes, and managed mirroring packages the log reader for you.

lessons.title: Orchestrating dependencies

lead.text: The tasks of a pipeline and the dependencies between them form a **directed graph**. Each task is a node, and an arrow from one task to another means that the second reads what the first writes, so it cannot start until the first has finished. In the figure three tasks each read from a different source, a join combines their outputs, and a last task publishes the result. The graph must also be **acyclic**, with no chain of arrows that leads back to its starting task, since a task that had to wait for itself could never run. A directed acyclic graph is shortened to **DAG**, and it is the structure that Apache Airflow and most other orchestration tools use to describe a pipeline.

Because there are no cycles, there is always at least one order in which every task runs after all the tasks it reads from. The three source tasks in the figure have no arrows between them, so any of them may go first, and the join and the publish step follow once they are done. Wherever an arrow does not force an order, the scheduler is free to run the tasks at the same time instead of one after another.

diagram.alt: A task graph with three source tasks of 4, 6 and 2 minutes, all feeding a join of 3 minutes, which feeds a publish task of 1 minute. A second view marks the longest chain, source 2, join and publish, totalling 10 minutes.
diagram.caption: The sources have no arrows between them, so they may run in any order. Use the buttons to mark the longest chain.

reveal.text: There are 6 orders of the three sources, and the join and publish follow in the only order they can.

lead.text: How long a pipeline takes depends on the dependencies as well as the durations. The five tasks in the figure take 4, 6, 2, 3 and 1 minutes, which is 16 minutes of work. A single worker runs the tasks in turn and takes all 16 minutes. Two workers can run the sources side by side, and the run ends after 10 minutes, and a third worker brings no further gain.

The reason is the longest chain of tasks that must run one after another. The second source, the join and the publish step form such a chain, 6 + 3 + 1 = 10 minutes, and no task on it can start before the one ahead of it has finished. This chain is the **critical path**, and its length is a floor beneath the run time that no number of workers can lower. A task off the critical path has slack. The third source needs 2 minutes, but it has 6 minutes before the join starts, so it can start late without delaying anything.

afterFigure.text: It follows that speeding up a task which is off the critical path does not shorten the run, while saving a minute on the critical path saves a minute overall, so tuning starts there.

reveal.text: The critical path runs through the slower of Y and Z, so the minimum is 3 + 8 + 2 = 13 minutes.
The waits are 2, 4 and 8 minutes, which add to 14. The next screen explains why waits grow and what a retry requires of a task.

lead.text: A task can fail for a reason that has nothing to do with its logic: a source is briefly unreachable, or a cluster is short of capacity. The usual answer is to retry the task a limited number of times, waiting between attempts and making each wait longer than the last. Doubling the wait each time is called **exponential backoff**, and waits of 2, 4 and 8 minutes give a struggling source more and more time to recover without the scheduler pressing on it.

Retrying carries a condition. A retry runs the task again against the same inputs, which is safe only if the task is [[idempotent|A step that leaves the destination in the same state whether it runs once or twice. Met in 'What a pipeline is'.]]. A task that appends rows and fails after writing half of them adds those rows a second time when it is retried, and the limit on attempts matters because a failure that is not temporary would otherwise be repeated for ever.

afterFigure.text: The retry limit also sets how long one task can hold up the pipeline. With three retries after the first attempt, a task that always fails costs the 14 minutes of waiting plus the time of its four attempts.

reveal.text: Four attempts take 20 minutes and the waits take 14, so 34 minutes pass before the scheduler gives up.

lead.text: A **backfill** reruns a pipeline for past periods, because a bug was fixed or a source was added and history has to be recomputed. It works only if every run knows which period it is for. A task that reads today's date from the clock produces today's data when it is rerun for last Tuesday, so the period must be a parameter that the scheduler passes in, often called the run's logical date, and each task must choose its input and its output by that parameter.

Once the period is a parameter the runs are independent, so they can go in parallel up to a limit that protects the source and the cluster. Take 20 daily partitions with at most 3 running at a time. They go in waves of 3, and the last wave holds only 2, so there are 7 waves, because 20 ÷ 3 is a little over 6 and a partly filled wave still takes as long as a full one. If every run takes 10 minutes and a wave starts when the one before has ended, the backfill takes 7 × 10 = 70 minutes.

afterFigure.text: Rounding up is the step that is easy to forget. A backfill of 21 partitions at 3 at a time fills 7 waves exactly, and a backfill of 22 needs an eighth wave for its last single run.

steps.headline: Find how long a backfill of 45 daily partitions takes, 6 at a time, when each run lasts 10 minutes.

workedSteps.text: Divide the partitions by the number that run at once, and round up, because a partly filled wave still takes a whole wave.
The last wave holds 3 partitions, which is fewer than 6, but it still lasts the length of one run.
Each wave takes 10 minutes. Work out the total time in minutes.

reveal.text: Twenty partitions at 5 at a time fill exactly 4 waves of 10 minutes, so the backfill takes 40 minutes. The limit matters as much as the run length.

lessons.orientation: Read a pipeline as a directed acyclic graph, find its critical path, and plan retries and a parallel backfill.
lessons.nextAction: Place data in a warehouse, a lake or a lakehouse, and follow it through the bronze, silver and gold layers.

blocks.text: Five tasks of 4, 6, 2, 3 and 1 minutes add up to 16 minutes of work, and whether the pipeline takes 16 minutes or 10 depends on which tasks have to wait for which. A scheduler can decide that only if it knows how long each task takes and which tasks read the output of which, because a task whose input has not yet been written cannot start.

The second of those facts is a graph, with a task at each node and an arrow wherever one task reads what another writes. It shows which tasks can run side by side and which chain of tasks sets the shortest possible run, and the same graph tells the scheduler what to do when a task fails and how to rerun a month of history that went wrong.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to count the valid orders of a task graph, find its critical path, and work out how long a retry limit or a parallel backfill takes.
intro.whyItMatters: A pipeline that has to finish before the morning is planned from its critical path, and one that has to be repaired is planned from its backfill.

recap.keyIdea: The critical path sets the shortest run time of a task graph, retries are safe only for idempotent tasks, and a backfill takes one run length for every wave of parallel runs.

blocks.text: You read a task graph as nodes and arrows with no cycles, counted the orders it allows, and found that its longest chain of dependent tasks is the floor under its run time. Retries with doubling waits give a failing task a chance to recover, provided the task is idempotent, and a backfill passes each run its own period and runs the periods in waves, rounding the number of waves up.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson steps back from the tasks to the places data lives, comparing warehouses, lakes and lakehouses.

lessons.title: Warehouses, lakes and lakehouses

steps.headline: Schema on write and on read

lead.text: A **data warehouse** stores its data in tables that its own engine manages, and it insists on a schema before it accepts a row: every column has a name and a type, and a row that breaks the rules is refused when it is loaded. This is called **schema-on-write**. A **data lake** keeps files in cheap object storage in whatever form they arrive, JSON, CSV or Parquet, and applies a schema only when something reads them, which is called **schema-on-read**.

The figure sends the same faulty row to both, an amount that arrives as the text n/a. The warehouse refuses it at load, so its table holds only rows that fit, and someone has to deal with the refusal at once. The lake accepts the file as it is, which makes loading easy and flexible, and the bad value surfaces later, when a query tries to read the column as a number and fails.

afterFigure.text: Each design moves the cost of a bad row to a different moment. Schema-on-write pays at load and gives readers a clean table. Schema-on-read keeps everything, including data nobody yet knows how to use, and leaves each reader to cope. A lake that has no structure, no owner and no tables turns into a dumping ground that no one trusts, so its freedom has to be matched by discipline, which the layers later in the lesson supply.

diagram.alt: A row whose amount is the text n/a sent to a warehouse and to a lake. The warehouse checks the schema at load and refuses the row. The lake accepts the file and the query that reads amount as a number fails later.
diagram.caption: The same bad row in two systems. Use the buttons to see where each one notices it.

reveal.text: The 120 faulty rows are refused, leaving 9,880 loaded. A lake would have accepted all 10,000 and failed later at query time.
One copy of 2 TB replaces three, saving 4 TB. The next screen shows what makes sharing possible.

lead.text: The warehouse and the lake have opposite weaknesses: the warehouse is dependable but keeps its data inside its own engine, and the lake is open but unreliable. A **lakehouse** combines the strengths. It keeps data in open files in a lake, in a format such as Parquet, and adds a **table format** on top that records which files make up each table and allows transactions, which the next lesson explains in detail. Because the files are open, different engines, such as a SQL engine and a Spark engine, can read the same copy, which is possible only because storage is kept separate from the compute that reads it.

The figure shows what the separation saves. When each of three engines needs its own copy of a 2 TB table, 6 TB are stored and the copies can drift apart. When all three read one shared copy, 2 TB are stored and every engine sees the same rows.

afterFigure.text: Warehouse and lakehouse are therefore partners on many platforms and not rivals. In Microsoft Fabric a lakehouse and a warehouse can work on the same Delta tables in OneLake, and Databricks offers a comparable pairing. These are examples, and the pattern matters more than the product names.

diagram.alt: Three engines reading a 2 terabyte table. With a copy for each engine, 6 terabytes are stored and the copies can drift apart. With one shared copy in open files plus a table format, 2 terabytes are stored and all engines see the same rows.

lead.text: Inside a lakehouse the data is usually kept in layers, commonly called the **medallion** layers. **Bronze** holds raw data exactly as it arrived, unchanged and only ever added to, so a faithful copy always exists to return to. **Silver** holds the cleaned version, with one row per event, typed columns and duplicates removed. **Gold** holds tables built for particular uses, such as revenue per day per region.

The layers are not three copies for their own sake, since each has a different contract with its readers. Bronze promises that nothing was lost, silver promises consistent and typed rows, and gold promises a number that is ready to use. In the figure 1,200 raw events become 1,050 silver rows once 150 duplicates are removed, and 12 gold rows once the events are totalled for 3 days and 4 regions.

diagram.alt: Three layers of a lakehouse. Bronze holds 1,200 raw events unchanged. Silver holds 1,050 rows with one typed row per event after 150 duplicates are removed. Gold holds 12 rows of revenue per day per region.

steps.headline: Decide which layer should hold a table of monthly revenue for the finance dashboard.

workedSteps.text: Ask who reads the table and in what shape. A dashboard reads totals and not single events.
Totals by month need clean rows, one per event, so the table is built from silver and not from the raw files.
A table built from silver for one particular use is the layer that holds ready-made results. Name that layer.

lead.text: It is a common mistake to treat a lake as somewhere to put files that need no design. Files with no names that mean anything, no owner and no tables cannot be trusted, and a lake in that condition is a dumping ground. The medallion layers, together with the table format, are the discipline that prevents it: each table has an owner, a schema and a contract, and a reader knows which layer to trust for which purpose.

The layers are also a way of matching a request to the right place. A raw audit copy of what arrived belongs in bronze. A cleaned customers table belongs in silver. Monthly revenue for a dashboard belongs in gold. An analyst who needs ad hoc features for a model usually starts from silver, which has the detail of bronze without its mess, and a request that cannot be placed in a layer usually means that its purpose has not yet been pinned down.

reveal.text: A faithful, unchanged copy of what arrived is the purpose of bronze.
One row for every combination of day and region gives 30 × 4 = 120 rows, far fewer than the events they summarise.

lessons.orientation: Choose between a warehouse, a lake and a lakehouse for a need, and place data in the bronze, silver or gold layer.
lessons.nextAction: Read a Delta or Iceberg commit history to find which files make up a table at any version.

blocks.text: A company keeps the events from its shop app as raw JSON files, a clean table with one row for each customer, and a monthly revenue table for the finance team. The three hold related facts, but they are kept for different readers, who need different promises from them: the archive has to be complete, the customer table has to be consistent, and the revenue table has to be quick to read and trustworthy.

Where data is kept decides which of those promises can be kept. A warehouse checks every row against a schema before accepting it, a lake keeps files in whatever form they arrive, and a lakehouse keeps open files that several engines can read, with layers inside it that hold the same data at different stages of cleaning. Knowing what each place promises lets you put a new table where its readers can trust it, and say what a faulty row or an extra copy of a table will cost.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to match a need to a warehouse, a lake or a lakehouse, apply schema-on-write and schema-on-read to a faulty row, and place a table in bronze, silver or gold.
intro.whyItMatters: Platform conversations are mostly about where data lives and how refined it is, and the answers decide what readers can trust.

recap.keyIdea: A warehouse checks schema on write, a lake on read, and a lakehouse keeps open files with a table format so engines share one copy, organised in bronze, silver and gold layers.

blocks.text: You compared a warehouse, which refuses a faulty row at load, with a lake, which accepts it and fails later, and saw that a lakehouse lets several engines read one transactional copy instead of three. The medallion layers then divide that copy by promise: bronze keeps raw data, silver holds clean typed rows, and gold holds tables built for a use.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson opens the table format that makes a lakehouse work, and reads a commit history to find a table's files at any version.

lessons.title: Open table formats

lead.text: Object storage can write whole files but cannot change them afterwards, so a table of Parquet files cannot be updated by editing a file. A **table format** gets round this by treating the data files as immutable and keeping a separate record of which files make up the table. In Delta Lake the record is a folder called `_delta_log` beside the data. Each change to the table is a **commit**, a small JSON file named for its version number, padded to 20 digits, such as `00000000000000000012.json`, and it lists the data files that the commit adds and those it removes.

To find the table at a given version, start with nothing and apply the commits from version 0 up to that version in order, adding each added file and dropping each removed one. The figure uses a history of four commits. At version 2 the live files are q, r and s, because the commit at version 2 removed p, and yet p is still on storage.

afterFigure.text: Two facts follow. A change, even one that touches most of the table, is only a small commit file and not a rewrite of the data. And a removed file is marked as removed and not erased, so its bytes stay where they were, which is what makes it possible to read an earlier version.

diagram.alt: A history of four commits. v0 adds files p and q, v1 adds r, v2 removes p and adds s, v3 removes q and r and adds t. Each view shows the commits applied up to one version, the live files, and the files on storage including removed ones.
diagram.caption: Pick a version to replay the log up to it. Dashed files are removed from the table but still stored.

lead.text: A table with thousands of commits would be slow to open if every reader replayed the log from version 0. To avoid that, the writer saves a **checkpoint** from time to time, a file that holds the complete list of live files at one version. A reader finds the latest checkpoint, loads it as its starting point, and applies only the commits that come after it.

With a checkpoint at version 20 and the latest commit at version 27, the reader applies versions 21 to 27, which is 7 commit files, and the first 20 commit files need not be read. A checkpoint changes how fast a table opens and not what it contains, because both routes arrive at the same set of files, and the log remains the authority.

reveal.text: The commits after the checkpoint are versions 21, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26 and 27, which is 7 files.
The winner creates version 5 and the loser retries as version 6, so the latest version is 6. The next screen explains how this works without a lock.

lead.text: Several writers may commit to one table at the same time, and the format does not lock the table. A writer works **optimistically**: it reads the current version, prepares its files, and then tries to create the next commit file, for example version 5. Creating a file whose name does not yet exist either succeeds or fails as a single step in the storage layer, so only one writer can create version 5. A writer that fails looks at what the winner changed. If the two changes do not conflict, for instance because they added different files, it retries as version 6, and if they do conflict, it fails and the work is redone.

Readers take no locks either. A query begins by fixing the version it will read, and it reads that **snapshot** from beginning to end, even if writers commit newer versions while it runs. Each query therefore sees a table that is consistent, with all of a commit's changes or none of them, which is the property known as snapshot isolation. Iceberg reaches the same result with a different structure, shown in the figure: a chain of metadata that ends in the data files, with a single pointer that a commit swaps from the old metadata to the new.

reveal.text: The query fixed its snapshot at version 12 when it started, so it reads version 12 throughout. A later query would read version 14.

lead.text: Deleting rows or rewriting files only marks files as removed in a commit, and the bytes stay on storage, so a table's storage grows even when its live size does not. Two maintenance jobs deal with that. **Compaction** rewrites many small live files into a few larger ones as a new commit, which adds the new file and removes the old ones, as version 3 does in the first figure where t replaces q and r. **Vacuum** physically deletes files that no version within a retention period needs, and in Delta the default retention is 7 days.

Old versions need old files, so the two jobs trade against **time travel**, which is reading the table as it was at an earlier version. After a vacuum, any version whose files were deleted can no longer be read, and the last figure shows the effect. The retention period is the length of history that is kept readable.

afterFigure.text: A table format is therefore not a database. It is metadata over immutable files, and the engines that read and write the files do the work, which is why Delta and Iceberg tables can be read by several engines.

lessons.orientation: Read a commit history to find a table's files at any version, and explain how optimistic commits give readers a consistent snapshot.
lessons.nextAction: Estimate how much data a filtered query reads under a partitioning scheme, and pick a partition column.

blocks.text: A table of several terabytes in object storage is only a folder of Parquet files, and object storage can write a file but cannot edit one, nor change several files in a single step. Yet lakehouse tables accept deletes and updates, give each query a consistent view while writers are busy, and can be read as they stood last Tuesday.

All of this comes from one small record kept beside the files, a log of which files belong to the table at each moment. The data files are never changed and the table is whatever the log says it is, so an update is a new entry that swaps some files in the list for others, and an old version is the list as it stood before. Reading that log tells you which files a query reads at any version, which files a cleanup job may safely delete, and why two writers working at once do not corrupt the table.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to replay a commit log to find a table's files at a version, count files on storage before and after a vacuum, and say why a query reads one consistent snapshot.
intro.whyItMatters: Every claim a lakehouse makes about transactions, history and cleanup follows from the commit log, so it is worth reading directly.

recap.keyIdea: A table format keeps immutable files and a log of commits, so a table at a version is the commits replayed in order, and removed files remain until a vacuum.

blocks.text: You replayed a log of commits to find the live files at a version, and saw that a checkpoint lets a reader skip the early commits. Writers commit optimistically by creating the next version, and readers fix one version and read it throughout. Compaction replaces small files with large ones, and vacuum deletes unreferenced files, which also ends time travel to the versions that needed them.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at how files are arranged inside a table, and at how much data a filtered query can skip.

lessons.title: Partitioning and file layout

lead.text: A **partition** is a group of a table's rows stored together in a folder of their own, chosen by the value of a **partition column**. A table of 1,200 GB partitioned by month, over one year, is twelve folders of about 100 GB each. The first view of the figure reads the table with no filter, and it has to open all twelve.

A query that filters on the partition column can open only the folders it needs and skip the rest without looking inside them, which is called **partition pruning**. A query for the second quarter reads 3 of the 12 folders, which is 300 GB, a quarter of the table. The benefit disappears when the filter is on some other column. The third view filters on a customer, and since the table is not partitioned by customer any month might hold a matching row, so all twelve folders are read.

afterFigure.text: Partitioning therefore does not speed up every query. It speeds up the queries that filter on the partition column and leaves the others as they were, and it has a cost in the number of files, which the next screens examine.

reveal.text: Two partitions of 100 GB are opened and the other ten are skipped, so the query reads 200 GB.
One partition holds 400 KB. That is tiny next to the 100 GB of a monthly partition, and the next screen explains why it matters.

lead.text: The number of distinct values in a column is called its **cardinality**, and it decides how many partitions there will be. A date has about 365 values a year, which divides a big table into folders that are each worth reading. A customer id may have millions of values, and a table partitioned by customer id would have a folder for each one.

The figure compares the two choices for the 1,200 GB table. By month each partition holds 100 GB, and with 3,000,000 customers each partition holds 1,200 GB ÷ 3,000,000 = 400 KB, far below the dashed line that marks a size worth reading on its own. The axis is logarithmic, so each step up is a thousand times larger and the real gap, a factor of 250,000, is much wider than it looks.

afterFigure.text: A column that is filtered on most is not automatically a good partition column. A good one is used in filters and also has few enough values that every partition stays large, and a date, a region or a month usually meets both tests.

reveal.text: `order_date` is used in the filters and has a moderate number of values, so each partition stays large.

lead.text: A very large number of very small files has a cost of its own. Reading a file means opening it, reading its footer and scheduling work for it, and when a file holds a few kilobytes these fixed costs outweigh the reading of the data. Small files come from partitioning by a column with too many values, and also from frequent small writes: a job that writes one file every 10 minutes into each of 8 partitions creates 8 × 144 = 1,152 files in a day.

The repair is **compaction**, which, as the previous lesson showed, rewrites many small files as a few large ones in a new commit. Compaction leaves the rows as they were and changes only the files that hold them, so it is worth scheduling after the writes that create small files, and a table that is written often needs it regularly.

reveal.text: Each partition gets 1,440 files in a day, and there are 5 partitions, so 7,200 files.

lead.text: Inside a partition, files can still be skipped. The footer of each Parquet file, and the metadata of a table format, records the smallest and largest value of each column in that file, and a query filtering on the column can rule out any file whose range does not include the value. This is **data skipping**, and it is the technique from the lesson on file formats applied across the files of a table.

The figure shows four files whose `order_id` ranges are 1 to 200, 150 to 420, 400 to 650 and 700 to 900. A filter on 410 falls inside both the second and the third range, since they overlap, so two files are read. A filter on 800 falls inside only the fourth, so one file is read. In the third view the same rows have been sorted by `order_id` before they were written, which gives four separate ranges, and the filter on 410 reads a single file.

afterFigure.text: Statistics skip files only when the ranges are narrow and separate. If rows arrive in random order, every file's range covers nearly the whole column and nothing can be skipped, so clustering the data on the filter column, as compaction can do, is what makes the statistics useful.

diagram.alt: Four files shown as bars on an order_id axis from 1 to 900 with a vertical filter line. In the unsorted layout the ranges overlap, and a filter at 410 reads two files while a filter at 800 reads one. After sorting by order_id the ranges are separate and a filter at 410 reads one file.

steps.headline: A 1,800 GB table is partitioned by day over 360 days. A query filters on the last 30 days. Work out how many gigabytes it reads.

workedSteps.text: Divide the table's size by the number of partitions to find one partition's size.
The filter names 30 days, so 30 partitions are opened and the other 330 are skipped.
Multiply the partitions opened by the size of one. Work out the gigabytes read.

reveal.text: The day's data is 7,200 × 4 MB = 28,800 MB, and 28,800 ÷ 200 = 144 files. Compaction cut the file count by a factor of 50.

lessons.orientation: Estimate how much data a filtered query reads under a partitioning scheme, and pick a partition column of the right cardinality.
lessons.nextAction: Count tasks, waves and shuffles, and see why one skewed key can set the run time of a whole stage.

blocks.text: A table of 730 GB holds three years of orders, and a report asks for the last week. If the files are laid out so that the report can tell which of them hold that week, it reads about 14 GB. If they are laid out without regard to date, it reads all 730 GB, and the query, the engine and the hardware are the same in both cases.

The layout is a decision about which rows share a folder and which share a file. Rows kept in folders by date let a filter on date skip every folder outside its range, and statistics kept for each file let it skip files inside a folder, but only when the values in each file are close together. With a table's size, its number of folders and the ranges in its files, you can work out how many gigabytes a filtered query will read before the layout is built, and see when a layout has been cut so finely that its files cost more to open than to read.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to estimate the bytes a filtered query reads under a partitioning scheme, choose a partition column of sensible cardinality, and use file ranges to say which files a filter can skip.
intro.whyItMatters: Layout is one of the few levers that changes the cost of a query by factors of ten or a hundred without changing the query.

recap.keyIdea: Partitioning lets a filter on the partition column skip folders, but a column with too many values makes tiny files, and file statistics skip files only when the ranges are narrow and separate.

blocks.text: You estimated the bytes read by a filter that names the partition column, and found that a filter on another column reads everything. A column with millions of values makes partitions of a few hundred kilobytes, whose fixed costs outweigh their data, and compaction repairs small files by rewriting them as large ones. Within a partition, min and max statistics skip files whose ranges miss the filter, and sorting makes the ranges narrow enough to do it well.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson moves from storage to computation, and asks how an engine divides the work into tasks and why one overloaded key can hold up a whole stage.

lessons.title: Distributed processing

lead.text: A distributed engine divides its input into **partitions**, pieces that can be processed independently, and runs one **task** for each partition. Spark by default cuts input files into pieces of about 128 MiB, so a file of 1.5 GiB, which is 1,536 MiB, gives 1,536 ÷ 128 = 12 partitions and therefore 12 tasks. The first view of the figure shows that cutting. The word partition is used twice in data engineering: a table's partitions, from the previous lesson, are folders grouped by a column's value, while an engine's partitions are the pieces of data that its tasks work on.

A cluster has a fixed number of cores, and each core runs one task at a time. If there are 12 tasks and 4 cores, the first 4 tasks start together, the next 4 start as those finish, and so on, in rounds called **waves**. The second view shows 3 waves. The number of waves is the number of tasks divided by the number of cores, rounded up, because a partly filled wave still has to be waited for.

afterFigure.text: Tasks and cores are the two numbers behind most estimates of a job's duration. When the tasks are of equal length, the run time is the number of waves multiplied by the time of one task, and adding cores shortens it only until there are as many cores as tasks.

diagram.alt: A file of 1.5 GiB cut into twelve pieces of 128 MiB, each becoming a task, and then the twelve equal tasks scheduled on four cores in three waves.
diagram.caption: From data to tasks to waves. Use the buttons to move between the two ideas.

100 ÷ 24 is a little over 4, and the partly filled last wave still takes a full round, so 5 waves.

lead.text: Some operations can be done on each partition without looking at any other. A filter keeps or drops rows one at a time, a select keeps some columns, and a union puts partitions side by side. Such an operation is a **narrow transformation**, because each output partition depends on a single input partition, and it runs inside the existing tasks without moving data between machines.

Other operations need rows with the same key to meet in one place. A group by a key must bring every row for that key to the same task, so every output partition reads from every input partition. This is a **wide transformation**, and the movement of data that it causes is a **shuffle**: each task on the writing side, a **map task**, splits its output into one block for every reducing partition, and the tasks on the reading side, the **reducers**, then fetch their blocks across the network. If 20 tasks write to 30 reducing partitions, they produce 20 × 30 = 600 blocks.

afterFigure.text: Shuffles are the expensive step in most jobs, because they use the network and the disks, so the amount of data shuffled and the number of blocks are worth counting. A join of two large tables is also wide, since rows with matching keys have to meet, and the last screens show a way to avoid it when one table is small.
