reveal.text: Each of the 80 tasks writes 200 blocks, so 80 × 200 = 16,000 blocks.
The hot key's task receives 350 million rows and needs 350 seconds. The other four finish long before. The next screen shows why this limits the whole stage.

lead.text: A shuffle sends every row with the same key to the same task. That works well when keys are spread evenly and badly when one key is much more common than the others. In the figure 500 million rows go to 5 reducers that each process 1 million rows per second. Spread evenly, each reducer would receive 100 million rows and finish in 100 seconds. When one key holds 70% of the rows, its reducer receives 350 million rows and needs 350 seconds, while the other four share the remaining 150 million rows and finish in under 40 seconds.

A stage is finished only when its slowest task is, so it takes 350 seconds, 3.5 times as long as the even split, with four of the five cores idle for most of that time. This is **data skew**. Adding machines does nothing for it, because the hot key still goes to one task. The remedies work on the key: spreading it over several tasks, a technique called salting, or avoiding the shuffle for that join altogether.

diagram.alt: Five reducers processing 500 million rows at 1 million rows per second each. Spread evenly each needs 100 seconds and the stage takes 100 seconds. When one key holds 70 percent of the rows, one reducer needs 350 seconds and the other four about 37.5 seconds each, so the stage takes 350 seconds.

workedSteps.text: The hot key's task receives 40% of the 1,000 million rows.
The other nine tasks share the other 600 million rows, which is about 67 million rows each, so they finish well before the hot task.
The stage lasts as long as the hot task, which processes 2 million rows per second. Work out the seconds.

lead.text: Spark does not run a transformation at the moment its line is written. Calls such as filter, select and group by only add a step to a plan, and the plan is executed when an **action** asks for a result, such as count, collect or writing the output. This is called **lazy evaluation**, and it lets the engine look at the whole plan before running anything, for example to read only the columns that the plan uses and to skip the partitions that a filter excludes.

A consequence is that a line which looks slow may cost nothing when it is written, while the first action pays for everything before it. When a job seems to stall on its last line, the cause is usually earlier in the plan, and the plan is where to look.

reveal.text: Filter and select only extend the plan. The call that returns a result to the program is the action.

lead.text: A join of two large tables is a wide operation, because rows with matching keys must meet, so both sides are shuffled. When one side is small, the engine can avoid the shuffle with a **broadcast join**, which sends a full copy of the small table to every **executor**, the process on each machine that runs the tasks. Each task then joins its own partition of the large table locally, and the large table does not move at all.

The saving can be worked out in advance. Broadcasting a 50 MB table to 10 executors moves 50 × 10 = 500 MB, whereas shuffling a 2 TB table moves terabytes. The limit is the size of the small table: a broadcast copy must fit in each executor's memory, and the engine chooses it only below a size threshold.

reveal.text: Each of the 8 executors receives its own 40 MB copy, so the broadcast moves 320 MB, a tiny amount next to a 1.5 TB shuffle.

lessons.orientation: Count tasks, waves and shuffle blocks, and explain why one skewed key can set the run time of a whole stage.
lessons.nextAction: Write the SQL that keeps the latest record per key, and see why deduplication must come before totals.

blocks.text: Ten gigabytes of data cannot be processed quickly by one worker reading it from top to bottom, so a distributed engine such as Spark cuts the data into pieces and gives each piece to a task running on a core somewhere in a cluster. The speed-up is real, but it is not the same as dividing the time by the number of machines.

The gap comes from things that can be counted before the job runs. The pieces are processed in rounds no wider than the cluster's cores, an operation that groups rows by key has to move data between machines before it can start, and the pieces are not always the same size. Counting them for a job tells you where its time goes, and so whether more machines, a different key or a different kind of join would make it faster.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to count the tasks and waves of a stage, classify an operation as narrow or wide, and estimate how long a stage with a skewed key takes.
intro.whyItMatters: Most slow jobs are slow for one of a few reasons, and each of them can be counted from the job's own numbers.

recap.keyIdea: An engine runs one task per partition in waves across its cores, wide operations shuffle data, and a stage lasts as long as its slowest task, so one hot key can set the run time.

blocks.text: You counted the tasks that a 6 GiB input produces, the waves that 100 tasks need on 24 cores, and the blocks a shuffle writes, 80 × 200 = 16,000. A shuffle sends all rows of a key to one task, so a key holding 60% of the rows makes a stage as slow as that one task, whatever the cluster size. Lazy plans, which start work only at an action, and broadcast joins, which move a small table instead of shuffling a large one, round out the picture.

lessons.title: Cleaning and deduplicating

lead.text: In a bronze table every load is kept, so an event that the source sends again appears again, with a later `loaded_at`. An event is identified by a key such as `event_id`, and the rows that share a key are duplicates of one event, although they need not be identical: the second copy may carry a corrected value, or padding in its amount, and it always has a new `loaded_at`.

The obvious tool, `SELECT DISTINCT`, removes only rows that are identical in every column. Two rows for event o17 that differ in `loaded_at` are different rows to `DISTINCT`, so both of them survive. What is needed is a rule that compares only the key and then chooses which row of the group to keep, which for re-sent data is usually the one loaded last, because it holds the source's latest word.

diagram.alt: Two rows for the same event o17 with the same amount, loaded on 05-01 and 05-02. SELECT DISTINCT treats them as different rows because loaded_at differs. Comparing only the key shows that they belong to one event.

reveal.text: Every re-sent row differs from its original in `loaded_at`, so `DISTINCT` treats all 500 rows as different and returns them all.

lead.text: To keep the latest row for each key, number the rows of each key from newest to oldest and keep number 1. A **window function** does the numbering without collapsing the rows: `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY reading_id ORDER BY loaded_at DESC)` works on each group of rows that share a `reading_id` separately, orders each group by `loaded_at` with the newest first, and gives every row its place in that order, which the query calls `rn`.

The figure runs it on six readings. Reading r1 was loaded twice, so its two rows get `rn` 1 and `rn` 2, and the row loaded on 06-02 is the one with `rn = 1`. Wrapping the numbering in a subquery and keeping `WHERE rn = 1` leaves exactly one row per reading, four in all, because a window function cannot be filtered in the same query level that creates it. The pattern of partitioning by the key, ordering by the load time and keeping `rn = 1` is the standard way to deduplicate in SQL.

afterFigure.text: Notice that reading r3 survives with its only row, a temperature of n/a. Deduplication decides which row to keep, and does not decide whether the row is any good, which is the job of the typing step later in the lesson.

queries.label: DISTINCT keeps all six
queries.sql:
SELECT DISTINCT * FROM bronze
ORDER BY reading_id, loaded_at;

queries.label: Rows numbered per reading
queries.sql:
SELECT reading_id, temp, loaded_at,
  ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
    PARTITION BY reading_id ORDER BY loaded_at DESC) AS rn
FROM bronze ORDER BY reading_id, rn;

queries.label: Keep rn = 1
queries.sql:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
    PARTITION BY reading_id ORDER BY loaded_at DESC) AS rn
  FROM bronze)
SELECT reading_id, sensor, temp, loaded_at
FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1 ORDER BY reading_id;

reveal.text: The order is newest first: 03-05 gets rn 1 and 03-02 comes next, so it gets rn 2.
The query adds all 450 rows, so it returns 4,500, which counts the 50 repeats. The next screen shows what that means for the order of the steps.

lead.text: The order in which cleaning steps run matters as much as the steps themselves. The day's bronze table holds 450 rows for 400 distinct events, since 50 events were sent twice, and every event is worth 10. Adding up the amounts first gives 450 × 10 = 4,500, a figure that includes the 50 repeats. Deduplicating first leaves 400 rows and a total of 4,000.

An aggregate cannot repair itself afterwards. Once rows have been added together the copies can no longer be told apart, so the total is already wrong when it is computed, and every report built on it inherits the error. The same holds for typing: a total over text that was cast carelessly is wrong at the moment it is computed, which is why cleaning happens in silver and totals are built in gold.

reveal.text: The excess is 4,500 − 4,000 = 500, and 500 as a share of 4,000 is 12.5%.

lead.text: Values arrive as text, with padding, mixed formats and the occasional word where a number belongs. Cleaning removes the padding with `TRIM` and converts the text with `CAST(... AS REAL)`, so that a value such as `' 10.50'` becomes 10.5. What a cast does with text that is not a number depends on the engine: SQLite gives 0 without any error, while other engines raise an error or return `NULL`. A quiet 0 is dangerous, because the row then adds zero to a sum and nobody is told.

The safe habit is to test each value before the cast and send the rows that fail to a **reject table**, which keeps the row, the reason it failed and a count. Dropping bad rows without a record leaves no evidence and no way to repair the source, whereas a reject table turns each failure into something that can be counted, reported and fixed.

reveal.text: The 14 failing rows leave the main flow and go to the reject table, so 960 − 14 = 946 rows continue.

steps.headline: Find the total of the latest amount per key in these rows: k1 5 (loaded 03-01), k1 6 (03-02), k2 4 (03-01), k2 4 (03-03), k3 9 (03-01).

workedSteps.text: Group the rows by key and order each group newest first. Keep `rn = 1` in each group.
Each key now has one row, so the repeats and the old value for k1 are gone. Summing all five rows would count them, and the total would be 28.
Add the three kept amounts. Work out the total.

reveal.text: Ascending order puts the oldest row first, so the kept row is the one loaded on 2026-03-01, the opposite of what deduplication intends.

blocks.text: A source sometimes sends a file again after correcting a mistake in it, and a bronze table, which keeps everything that arrives, then holds every order from that file twice. A query that adds up the day's revenue over that table returns a figure that is too high by the amount of the re-sent orders, and nothing in the query says so.

Cleaning is the work of turning a table like that into one where each fact appears once and every value has a type, before any figure is built from it. It decides which of two copies of an order to keep, converts text such as ' 10.50' into a number, and sets aside the rows that cannot be converted, and it has to do all of this before anything is added up, since a total cannot tell which of its rows were copies. Done in that order, it gives a revenue figure that counts each order once, together with a record of every row that was left out and why.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to write the SQL that keeps the latest row per key, explain why DISTINCT does not do that job, and say why deduplication comes before totals.
intro.whyItMatters: A total built on uncleaned rows is wrong at the moment it is computed, and no later step can correct it.

recap.keyIdea: Duplicates are rows that share a key, `ROW_NUMBER` with `rn = 1` keeps the latest of each, and deduplication must precede aggregation so that no total counts a repeat.

blocks.text: You saw that `DISTINCT` keeps a re-sent record whose load time differs, and that numbering each key's rows newest first and keeping `rn = 1` leaves one row per key. A sum taken before that step counted 450 rows for 400 events and overstated revenue by 12.5%. Text is trimmed and cast before use, and rows that fail go to a reject table with their reasons, so that nothing is dropped without a count.

lessons.title: Streaming and event time

lead.text: Every record in a stream has two times. Its **event time** is when the thing happened, as recorded at the source, which is 10:04 for the purchase in the figure. Its **processing time** is when the pipeline sees it, 10:11 after the delay in the lift. In a batch job over yesterday's data the two never conflict, because everything has arrived, but in a stream they differ by a delay that nobody controls.

Counting purchases per five-minute window by processing time puts this purchase in the window that starts at 10:10, so the count for 10:00 to 10:05 is too low and the one for 10:10 too high, and a rerun of the same data on a day with different delays gives different counts. Windows by event time put the purchase where it happened, and the answers stay the same however late the records arrive, which is why streaming engines window by event time. The price is that a window can never be sure it has seen every record, a problem that the watermark addresses later in this lesson.

afterFigure.text: This separation of event time from processing time was set out in Google's Dataflow model paper of 2015, and the stream engines that followed it, Spark Structured Streaming among them, adopted its vocabulary.

diagram.alt: A time line from 10:00 to 10:20 in five-minute windows. A purchase happened at 10:04 and reached the pipeline at 10:11. Windowed by processing time it is counted in the 10:10 window. Windowed by event time it is counted in the 10:00 window.

reveal.text: The events at 09:11, 09:12 and 09:19 fall in that window, which is 3 events. 09:21 belongs to the next window.

lead.text: A **tumbling window** cuts time into equal, separate intervals, such as every five minutes, and each event falls in exactly one of them. A **sliding window** has a length and a smaller step, so a 10-minute window that starts every 5 minutes overlaps its neighbours, and each event falls in 10 ÷ 5 = 2 windows. A **session window** has no fixed length: it groups events that follow each other closely and closes when no event has arrived for a set gap, such as 5 minutes.

The figure places six events, at minutes 1, 3, 4, 12, 14 and 22, under each kind. The tumbling five-minute windows count 3, 0, 2, 0, 1 and 0 events. The sliding windows count every event twice, in the window that contains it and in the one that starts 5 minutes earlier. The session windows give 3 sessions, because the pauses from minute 4 to 12 and from 14 to 22 are longer than the 5-minute gap.

afterFigure.text: A sliding window is how a moving average is computed over a stream, and a session window is how a visit to a website is found, since a visit has no fixed length.

diagram.alt: Six events at minutes 1, 3, 4, 12, 14 and 22 grouped three ways. Tumbling 5-minute windows give counts 3, 0, 2, 0, 1, 0. Sliding 10-minute windows every 5 minutes put each event in two windows. Session windows with a 5-minute gap give three sessions.

reveal.text: The window length divided by the step gives the number of windows an event belongs to: 12 ÷ 4 = 3.
A pause of 5 minutes or more starts a new session. The pauses are 2→8, 9→15 and 16→30, each at least 5, so there are 4 sessions.
The watermark is 11:20 minus 15 minutes, which is 11:05. The next screen explains what the engine does with it.

lead.text: Because records can arrive late, the engine has to decide when it has waited long enough to report a window. It does so with a **watermark**, a moving threshold in event time. The engine tracks the latest event time it has seen and subtracts an allowed lateness that the developer chooses, and the result is the watermark. With a latest event time of 10:21 and an allowed lateness of 10 minutes, the watermark is 10:11, and every window that ends before 10:11 can be finalised, because the engine no longer expects records for it.

The figure follows one stream. The watermark rises only as later events arrive, so a quiet period does not close windows. In the last view an event stamped 10:08 arrives when the watermark is at 10:11, and the window from 10:00 to 10:10 is already closed. Spark's guide states the guarantee with care: a watermark of 10 minutes means the engine will never drop data that is less than 10 minutes late, but data that is later than that may or may not be processed.

afterFigure.text: A longer allowed lateness keeps windows open for longer, which catches more late records and also delays the results and holds more state in memory. The setting trades completeness against latency, and the right value depends on how late records really arrive.

diagram.alt: An event-time line from 10:00 to 10:30 with three ten-minute windows. After events at 10:03 and 10:12 the watermark is 10:02 and every window is open. After an event at 10:21 it is 10:11 and the first window closes. A late event stamped 10:08 then arrives too late to count.
diagram.caption: The watermark is the latest event time minus 10 minutes. Use the buttons to follow the stream.

workedSteps.text: Work out the watermark.
The event belongs to the window from 14:00 to 14:05, and that window ended before the watermark, so it has been closed.
Find how far the event's time is behind the watermark, in minutes: the difference between 14:31 and 14:03.

lead.text: A stream is read from a log of numbered records, and each record has an **offset**. A consumer that has processed records remembers its place by committing an offset, and after a crash it restarts from the last committed offset. If it processed some records after that commit and crashed before committing again, those records are read a second time. This is **at-least-once** delivery: every record is processed, and some are processed more than once. Committing first and processing afterwards gives the opposite, **at-most-once**, in which a crash loses records.

Exactly-once results are what everyone wants, and they are not free. Since the source replays after a failure, the effect on the destination is exactly once only if the sink tolerates the replay. A sink that appends rows duplicates every replayed record, while an idempotent sink, such as an upsert on a key, absorbs them, which is the property from the first lesson. The figure shows 5 records replayed in each case.

diagram.alt: A log of records at offsets 38 to 48 with a committed offset of 40. The consumer processed offsets 40 to 44 and crashed before committing again. After restarting from 40, those five records are read again. An appending sink stores them twice, while an upsert sink replaces the same rows.
diagram.caption: What a replay does to two kinds of sink. Use the buttons to compare.

lessons.orientation: Assign events to tumbling, sliding and session windows, compute a watermark, and explain what at-least-once delivery means for an idempotent sink.

blocks.text: A phone records a purchase at 10:04, loses its signal in a lift, and uploads the record at 10:11. A stream that counts purchases for each five-minute window ought to count this one in the window from 10:00 to 10:05, and yet by the time the record arrives that window may already have been reported.

Streaming systems live in the gap between when something happened and when the system learns of it. The vocabulary of event time, windows and watermarks exists to say how long the system waits for late records, and what it does with the ones that miss the wait.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to assign events to windows, compute a watermark and say which windows it closes, and count the records a consumer replays after a failure.
intro.whyItMatters: Streaming results depend on how late data is handled, and the settings that decide it are simple enough to work out by hand.

recap.keyIdea: Windows follow event time, a watermark of latest event time minus allowed lateness decides when a window closes, and at-least-once delivery means the sink must tolerate replays.

blocks.text: You placed events in tumbling, sliding and session windows by their event time, and found that the watermark, the latest event time less the allowed lateness, tells the engine which windows may close. Delivery from a replayable log is at-least-once, so a consumer that crashed after committing offset 300 reads the records since then again, and only an idempotent sink makes the result exact.

lessons.title: Checking data in motion

lead.text: A **validation gate** is a check placed between two steps of a pipeline. It tests a batch of data against rules and then decides what happens to it. Typical rules are that a key is never null, that a key is unique, that an amount lies in a plausible range, and that the number of rows is close to what the previous run delivered. Gates are placed where data changes hands, when a file lands, when bronze becomes silver and when silver becomes gold, because each of those is a point where a different team or system takes responsibility for the data.

A gate can take one of two actions. It can **quarantine** the failing rows, writing them with the reason to a separate table and letting the rest continue, or it can **fail fast**, stopping the run and alerting someone before any bad data is published. The choice depends on how many rows fail. A few failing rows out of 2,000 are an exception that can be set aside, whereas a large share suggests that something upstream is broken and the whole batch should not be trusted. A **threshold**, such as 2% of the batch, is the line between the two, as the figure shows.

afterFigure.text: Failing fast keeps yesterday's good data in place instead of replacing it with today's wrong data, which is almost always the better outcome for the people reading the tables.

diagram.alt: A pipeline step with a validation gate between bronze and silver for a batch of 2,000 rows. With 20 failing rows, 1 percent against a 2 percent threshold, the rows go to quarantine and 1,980 continue to silver. With 100 failing rows, 5 percent, the run stops and an alert is raised.

The query names a column that has gone, so it fails. The next screen sorts schema changes into safe and breaking ones.

lead.text: The **schema** of a source, its columns and their types, is a contract that every reader of the data relies on. When the source changes it, the readers either keep working or break, and the changes fall into two groups. A change is **safe** when every query written against the old schema gives the same answer on the new one. Adding a nullable column is safe, because old queries do not mention it, and so is widening an integer to a bigint, because every old value still fits. A change is **breaking** when some existing query fails or changes its answer. Dropping a column breaks every query that selects it, renaming a column does the same, and changing text to a number breaks code that expects text.

Whether an added column is safe depends on its meaning as well as its name. A new column that changes what an existing join key means, or that multiplies rows because it is not unique, is breaking even though it only adds to the table. The figure shows three changes beside a query that reads the old schema.

diagram.alt: Three schema changes to an orders table. Adding a nullable column leaves an existing query working. Renaming cust to customer_id makes a query that selects cust fail. Changing a text column to an integer breaks a query that treats it as text.

reveal.text: Every old value fits in the wider type and old queries return the same results, so the change is safe.

lead.text: A pipeline can respond to a schema change in three ways. It can fail, stopping at the gate until someone decides. It can evolve, accepting the new column on purpose and updating the tables downstream. Or it can adapt silently, taking in whatever arrives. Silent adaptation is tempting and is the dangerous one, because a bug at the source then moves into every downstream table without anyone seeing it.

A sensible default is to detect the change at the landing gate, to accept the safe kinds automatically when the team has agreed to that, and to stop on the breaking kinds. Stopping costs a delay, and a wrong table that nobody notices costs a great deal more. The same reasoning applies to row-level checks, where the choice between quarantine and stopping rests on how many rows fail.

reveal.text: 2% of 4,000 is 80, so up to 80 failing rows pass and 81 would stop the run.

steps.headline: Decide what a 2% gate does with a batch of 5,000 rows that has 30 null keys, 60 negative amounts and 20 duplicate keys.

workedSteps.text: Add up the rows that fail a check. No row fails two checks, so the counts add.
Divide by the batch size to find the share that fails. Work out the percentage.
Compare with the 2% threshold. Above it, the gate stops the run and alerts someone instead of quarantining.

reveal.text: 4% of 2,000 is 80 failing rows, which is under the 5% threshold, so the gate quarantines them and 2,000 − 80 = 1,920 rows continue.

lessons.orientation: Place validation gates in a pipeline, classify a schema change as safe or breaking, and decide whether a batch passes a rejection threshold.
lessons.nextAction: Compute freshness and throughput against a target, and diagnose a slow or failing job from its symptoms.

blocks.text: A nightly file of orders arrives in which a few hundred rows have no customer key. Nothing in the pipeline fails: the load accepts the rows, the join to the customers table quietly leaves them out, and weeks later the revenue on a dashboard is lower than the finance team's figure by an amount that nobody can trace. Each step did what it was told, and no step was told to look at what it was given.

A check placed where data changes hands turns that silent loss into a decision made on purpose, to stop the run, to set the bad rows aside, or to let the batch through. Which of those is right depends on how many rows fail and on whether the source has changed the shape of its data, and both can be settled from the batch itself before anything reaches the tables that people read.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to classify a schema change as safe or breaking, compute the share of a batch that fails, and say whether a gate should quarantine or stop.
intro.whyItMatters: Checks are cheap next to the cost of a wrong table that readers trust, and they are what make failing fast and recovering possible.

recap.keyIdea: A validation gate quarantines a few failing rows or stops the run when the failing share passes a threshold, and a schema change is safe only if every existing query keeps its answer.

blocks.text: You placed gates between layers and compared the share of failing rows with a threshold: 1.6% of 2,500 rows was set aside and 2,460 continued, while 2.2% of 5,000 stopped the run. Renaming a column breaks queries that name it, whereas adding a nullable column or widening an integer leaves them working, and a pipeline should stop on breaking changes and not adapt to them silently.

lessons.title: Monitoring and tuning

lead.text: The first measure is **freshness**, the age of the newest data in a table at the moment someone looks at it. A table last loaded at 03:40 and checked at 12:15 is 8 hours 35 minutes old. If the service target says that the data may be at most 8 hours old, it is 35 minutes late, and the lateness is measured against that target and not against the time the job was scheduled.

Freshness is a property of the data and not of the job. In the second view of the figure every run succeeded, and still two of the five mornings breach the 6-hour target, because the source delivered late on those days. A pipeline that is on time with late inputs produces stale tables, which is why the check has to look at the newest timestamp in the data and not at the job's status.

diagram.alt: Bars showing the age of a table at 09:00 on five mornings against a target of 6 hours. Monday 5 h 10 min, Tuesday 5 h 40 min, Wednesday 6 h 35 min, Thursday 4 h 30 min, Friday 7 h 20 min. Wednesday and Friday breach the target. A second view marks every run as successful.

reveal.text: From 03:40 to 12:15 is 8 hours 35 minutes, which is 515 minutes. The target is 480 minutes, so the table is 35 minutes late.

lead.text: The second measure is **throughput**, the amount of data a job moves in a unit of time. A job that moves 150 million rows in 25 minutes, which is 1,500 seconds, has a throughput of 150,000,000 ÷ 1,500 = 100,000 rows per second. Dividing by seconds and not by minutes keeps the unit a rate that can be compared from one job to another.

Throughput links the size of the data to the deadline. If 600 million rows must be through in a window of 40 minutes, which is 2,400 seconds, the job needs 600,000,000 ÷ 2,400 = 250,000 rows per second, and a job that runs at 200,000 will miss the window. **Latency** is a different measure: the time one record takes to travel from the source to the destination. A nightly batch job can have high throughput and a latency of hours, and a streaming job can have the opposite.

reveal.text: 20 minutes is 1,200 seconds, and 240,000,000 ÷ 1,200 is 200,000 rows per second.

The job succeeded on time, so only the row count shows the problem: 600,000 is half of 1,200,000, which is 50% of the usual volume. The next screen names this signal and the others that sit beside it.

lead.text: Four signals cover most failures. **Freshness** asks whether the data is as new as promised. **Volume** asks whether the job wrote about the usual number of rows. **Duration** asks whether it took about as long as usual, which is throughput seen from the other side. **Failures and retries** ask whether tasks failed, and how often they had to run again. A job that succeeds with half the usual rows is also broken, so each signal is compared with what is normal for that table at that time, for example by alerting when a run writes less than 80% of its usual rows.

Monitoring only failures misses most of this. Failure is the one signal that the scheduler reports by itself, and the other three have to be measured from the data and from the run history. An alert is most useful when it names the table and the rule that fired, so that whoever receives it can tell at once which of the signals is out of range.

When a job is slow or wrong, the symptoms usually point to one of a few causes. If one task runs far longer than its siblings, the likely cause is **skew**, a key holding most of the rows, as in the lesson on distributed processing. If a table has thousands of tiny files and queries are slow to start, the cause is the small-files problem, and compaction is the repair. If a query with a filter scans the whole table, the layout does not match the filter, and partitioning or clustering on the filter column is the fix. If the output is empty or short while the job reports success, the source and the gates are where to look, and if tasks fail and retry repeatedly, the log of the failing task says whether a dependency or memory is the cause.

Adding capacity is the tempting response to slowness, and it is usually the last one to try. More cores do not shorten a skewed stage, because one task still holds the hot key, and they do not make a table of tiny files cheaper to open. Fixes to the layout and the key cost less, and they last, whereas extra capacity is paid for every night. The figure shows four dashboards and the cause each one points to.

diagram.alt: Four run dashboards and their likely causes. One task far slower than the others points to data skew. Thousands of tiny files point to the small-files problem. A successful run with empty output points to a missing input. Repeated retries point to a failing dependency.

steps.headline: A table was last loaded at 23:20 and is checked at 05:45 the next morning. Its target is 5 hours 20 minutes. Find out whether it is late, and by how much.

workedSteps.text: Find the age of the table. From 23:20 to midnight is 40 minutes, and from midnight to 05:45 is 5 hours 45 minutes.
Convert the age and the target to minutes.
Subtract the target from the age. Work out how many minutes late the table is.

lessons.orientation: Compute throughput and freshness against a service target, and diagnose a slow or failing job from its symptoms.
lessons.nextAction: Trace a change from development to production, and choose the access control that fits a protection need.

blocks.text: A nightly pipeline can finish on schedule, report success, and still leave the dashboard showing yesterday's numbers, because the source delivered late, or because the job wrote half the usual rows, or because it ran so slowly that it only just met its deadline. Each of those is a failure that the scheduler's own status cannot see.

Monitoring measures what matters to the people who read the data: how old the newest row in a table is, how many rows a run wrote compared with a usual night, and how long the run took. Each of those is a subtraction or a division against a baseline, and each one, when it goes wrong, points to a cause such as a late source, a skewed key or a table of tiny files. Knowing which measurement points to which cause lets you notice a bad night before the readers do and fix the cause instead of buying more machines.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to compute freshness and throughput against a target, choose the signals worth alerting on, and match a slow job's symptom to its likely cause.
intro.whyItMatters: A pipeline that is monitored only for failure will be wrong for days before anyone notices.

recap.keyIdea: Freshness, volume, duration and failures show whether a pipeline is healthy, and a job's symptoms point to causes such as skew or tiny files that layout and key fixes cure more cheaply than capacity.

blocks.text: You measured freshness as the age of the newest data against a target, and throughput as rows divided by seconds, and found that a job can succeed while delivering stale or half-empty tables. Four signals watch for that, and a slow task, a mass of tiny files, an empty output and repeated retries each point to a cause. Fixing the layout or the key is the first resort, and extra capacity the last.

recap.nextHook: The final lesson follows a pipeline from development to production, and chooses the access control and the secret handling that protect it.

lessons.title: Environments, security and release

lead.text: A pipeline lives in several **environments**, copies of the whole setup that serve different purposes. In **development** engineers change things freely and sometimes break them. In **test** the pipeline runs against a sample of the data, often a small share such as 1%, so that its results can be checked cheaply. In **production** it runs on the full data, and its tables are the ones that people rely on. A change moves through them in that order, which is called **promotion**.

The code of the pipeline is the same in all three. What differs is a set of **parameters**, such as the connection to the source and the location of the destination, which each environment supplies for itself. With three environments and the two parameters in the figure, a source and a destination, there are 3 × 2 = 6 values to keep, and none of them is written into the pipeline's code. The figure shows the path and a table of parameters.

afterFigure.text: In Microsoft Fabric, deployment pipelines and Git integration cover promotion and version control, and other platforms have their own tools. The practice is the same, and the product names are examples.

diagram.alt: A promotion path from a repository's main branch to development, test and production, and a table of parameters per environment. The pipeline code is the same in every environment, and each supplies its own source and destination.

lead.text: Pipeline definitions are kept in a **version control** repository, as text files, so that every change has an author, a date and a reason, and can be reverted. A change is made on a **branch**, a separate line of work, and is proposed for **review**, in which a colleague reads the difference before it is merged into the main branch. Merging to main triggers deployment to test, where the pipeline runs on the sample and its checks are run. Only when they pass is the change promoted to production.

The sequence is therefore branch, review, merge, deploy to test, validate, promote. It is slower than fixing a bug by editing production directly, and that is the point: a direct edit skips the review and the test, leaves no record of what changed, and cannot be undone by reverting a commit. A genuine emergency fix still follows the path, with a shorter review.

reveal.text: Merging triggers deployment to test, where the pipeline runs on a sample and its checks run, before anything reaches production.
Each region has 12,000 ÷ 4 = 3,000 rows, so the manager should see 3,000. The next screen names the control that does this.

lead.text: Not everyone who can use a table should see all of it, and the controls that decide this work at different levels. **Least privilege** is the starting rule: each person and each pipeline receives the smallest role that lets them do the work, so that a mistake or a stolen account does limited harm. **Row-level security** filters the rows a person can see, so that a regional manager who may see only EMEA sees only those rows of a shared table. **Column-level security**, or **masking**, hides or obscures particular columns, so that an analyst who may see orders but not customers' emails sees a masked value in place of the address. Sharing a table **read-only** lets a reader query it without being able to change it.

The figure uses the table of 12,000 orders from four regions. Row-level security gives the EMEA manager 3,000 of the 12,000 rows, with every column, whereas column-level security gives the analyst all 12,000 rows with the email column masked. The two controls answer different questions, which rows and which columns, and a table often needs both.

afterFigure.text: Giving everyone workspace administrator rights to avoid access problems is the opposite of least privilege. It makes every mistake a possible disaster and every stolen account a total loss.

reveal.text: The restriction is on a column, not on any set of rows, so it needs a control that works on columns.

lead.text: A pipeline needs credentials to reach its source and its destination, such as a database password or an access key. The worst place for one is the pipeline's own text, a notebook or a repository, because everyone who can read the notebook or the history then holds the credential, and deleting it later does not remove it from the history. A **secret store** is a service built to hold credentials. The pipeline is given an identity of its own, asks the store for the secret at run time, and the secret never appears in the code or in the logs.

Each environment has its own secrets, and the parameter table from the start of the lesson holds only the names of the secrets, not their values. Promoting a pipeline from test to production then changes which secret is looked up and does not move a password from one place to another, and rotating a secret means changing it in one place.

reveal.text: Everyone who can read the notebook or the repository holds the password, so 12 + 30 = 42 people.

steps.headline: Count the parameter values kept for a pipeline in 3 environments that each supply a source, a destination, a secret name and a sample size.

workedSteps.text: The pipeline's code does not change between environments, so none of the values is written into it.
Each environment supplies its own value for each parameter.
Multiply to find the number of values to keep. Work out the total.

reveal.text: The auditor needs to read and nothing more, which is the smallest role that does the job.

lessons.orientation: Explain how a pipeline moves from development to production under version control, and choose the access control and secret handling that fit a need.
lessons.nextAction: Design a pipeline as a graph, load and store its data safely, process and check it, and keep it monitored, secured and released under control.

blocks.text: A pipeline is defined by a handful of text files: the SQL for each step, a schedule, and settings that name its source, its destination and the password it uses to reach them. Over the years it runs, those files are changed many times by many people, and every change reaches the production tables, the ones that dashboards and reports read, by some route. A change pasted straight into production skips any review, leaves no record of what changed and cannot be undone by reverting it, whereas a change that passes through a review and a run on test data is caught before anyone reads the result.

The same files raise two more questions, which are who may read which rows and columns of the tables they produce, and where the password is kept, since a password written into a notebook can be read by everyone who can open the notebook. The release path, the access controls and the secret store are the answers, and with them you can say how any change should reach production and how much of a table any reader should see.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to put the steps of a release in order, match a protection need to row-level security, column-level security or read-only access, and say where a credential belongs.
intro.whyItMatters: The earlier lessons make a pipeline correct, and this one keeps it correct as it changes hands.

recap.keyIdea: A change reaches production by branch, review, test and promotion with parameters per environment, access follows least privilege, and credentials live in a secret store.

blocks.text: You followed a change from a branch through review, test and promotion, with the same code and a separate set of parameters in each environment. Row-level security gave a manager 3,000 of 12,000 rows, column-level security masked an email column, and read-only access served an auditor. Credentials belong in a secret store that the pipeline reads at run time, and never in a notebook or repository.

questions.prompt: The join reads 2,350 cleaned orders and a 60-row product list, and every order matches exactly one product. How many rows does the join write?
hints: Think about what a join does to each order row.
An order that matches exactly one product gives exactly one output row.
The product list supplies extra columns, not extra rows.
questions.onCorrect: The join widens each order row with the product's columns, so the row count stays at the number of orders.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two tables together, as stacking them would. A join pairs each order with its product instead.
That counts the products. The output has one row for each order.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A join attaches the product's columns to each order that matches it, so each of the 2,350 orders produces one row: 2,350 rows.

questions.prompt: A job reads the file of yesterday's orders at 02:00 every night. Which processing rhythm is it?
hints: Does the job work on a fixed set of data or on a flow with no end?
A complete file read on a schedule has a start and an end.

acceptedIdeas: Batch, because it processes a bounded set of data on a schedule
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Batch, because it processes a bounded set of data on a schedule

questions.onCorrect: The file holds a bounded set of orders and the job runs on a schedule, which makes it batch work.

misconceptions.feedback: Running every day does not make a job a stream. Each run reads a complete file with a beginning and an end, and a stream handles records as they arrive, with no last record to wait for.
A micro-batch runs every few seconds or minutes, so that it behaves almost like a stream. One run a night over a whole day of orders is ordinary batch work.

choices.label: Batch, because it processes a bounded set of data on a schedule
Streaming, because it runs every day without end
Micro-batch, because each run handles only one day

questions.prompt: A pipeline following ELT lands 2,500 raw rows, and cleaning finds 75 unusable rows. How many rows does the raw table hold once cleaning has run?
hints: Under ELT, which table is loaded first?
Cleaning writes its result to another table.
The raw table is not changed by the cleaning step.
questions.onCorrect: Cleaning writes to a second table, so the raw table keeps every row it was loaded with and the cleaning can be rerun.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the cleaned table. In ELT the raw table is loaded first and left as it is.
That is the number of unusable rows. The raw table keeps every row it was loaded with.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: ELT loads the raw rows first and cleans them into a separate table, so the raw table still holds all 2,500 rows.

questions.prompt: A job inserts three order rows into an empty table, which has no key declared, using plain `INSERT` statements. The orchestrator, the tool that schedules and retries the steps, reports a timeout and runs the job again, although the first run had in fact finished. What does the table hold afterwards?
hints: What does a plain `INSERT` do when an identical row is already in the table?
Think about what each run adds.

acceptedIdeas: Six rows, three of them copies of the other three
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Six rows, three of them copies of the other three

questions.onCorrect: A plain `INSERT` adds rows whether or not they are already there, so a retry doubles the data.

misconceptions.feedback: Writing the same rows again only replaces them if something matches each new row to an old one. A plain `INSERT` does no matching, so each run adds its rows to whatever is already there.
An `INSERT` can fail on a repeated row only when the table declares a key for it to clash with. This table has none, so the second run succeeds and adds three more rows.

choices.label: Three rows, because the second run fails on rows that are already there
Six rows, three of them copies of the other three
Three rows, because the second run writes the same rows again

questions.prompt: After the second run of the upsert, how many rows does the table hold?
hints: Which ids exist after the first run?
Does any id in the batch fail to match an existing row?
Rows that match are replaced, not added.
questions.onCorrect: Matching keys are replaced, so a second run of the same batch changes nothing, which is what idempotent means.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what plain INSERTs would give, because every run would add its rows. An upsert replaces rows with matching keys.
That adds the batch a second time. Rows whose keys already exist are replaced, not added.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: After the first run the ids are 10, 11, 12 and 13. The second run matches all four and adds none, so the table holds 4 rows.

questions.prompt: A step deletes the rows for 2026-05-02 and inserts that day's 3 rows. The table held 7 rows for earlier days, and the step runs twice. How many rows does the table hold?
hints: What does the delete remove at the start of the second run?
Count the rows for earlier days.
Add the 3 rows of the day that were written last.
questions.onCorrect: The delete clears what the first run wrote, so the second run ends in the same state and the step is safe to retry.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the second run as adding 3 more rows. The delete removed the first run's rows before they were written again.
That leaves out the 3 rows for 2026-05-02 that the last insert wrote.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each run deletes the day's rows before writing them again, so after either run the table has 7 + 3 = 10 rows.

questions.prompt: A card payment must have a fraud score within a second of arriving. Which processing style fits?
hints: Think about how long the data may wait before it is processed.
A batch waits for its schedule.
questions.onCorrect: A score within a second means each payment is handled as it arrives, which only streaming does.

misconceptions.feedback: A nightly batch scores payments hours after they arrive, long after the one-second limit.
A weekly batch waits even longer than a nightly one.
A manual export depends on a person and has no timing guarantee.

choices.label: Weekly batch
Streaming
Nightly batch
Manual export

questions.prompt: A step appends yesterday's rows to a table, and running it twice doubles the rows. Which property is missing? Give the one word.
hints: The property says a rerun leaves the destination unchanged.
It is the property that upserts and overwrites have and plain inserts lack.
questions.onCorrect: A step with idempotence leaves the same state after two runs as after one, which a plain append cannot do.

misconceptions.feedback: Atomicity means a step either completes or does not. The missing property is about what a second run does.

questions.prompt: Which description is ELT?
hints: ELT puts the load before the transform.
Where does the transform code run in ELT?
questions.onCorrect: ELT lands the raw data first and transforms it inside the destination, so the raw copy remains available.

misconceptions.feedback: That cleans first and loads only the result, which is ETL.
That changes the data at the source, before any pipeline has read it.
ELT still transforms the data. It does so after the load, inside the destination.

choices.label: Transform data while it is being typed into the source.
Load raw files into the lakehouse first, then transform them with SQL there.
Clean the data on a separate server, then load only the cleaned result.
Load the data and never transform it.

acceptedIdeas: Load raw files into the lakehouse first, then transform them with SQL there.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Load raw files into the lakehouse first, then transform them with SQL there.

questions.prompt: A columnar file has 50,000,000 rows. A query needs 3 columns of 8 bytes per value. How many gigabytes (10^9 bytes) does the reader fetch, ignoring compression?
hints: How many bytes does one column take?
Multiply the rows by the 8 bytes of each value.
Multiply by the number of columns and convert to gigabytes.
questions.onCorrect: The reader fetches only the three columns it needs, so the other columns cost nothing.

misconceptions.feedback: That treats the file as holding every column. A columnar reader fetches only the 3 it needs.
That is the size of a single column. The query needs three.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each column holds 50,000,000 values of 8 bytes, which is 400,000,000 bytes, and 3 columns make 1,200,000,000 bytes, or 1.2 GB.

questions.prompt: A file stores the `order_id` column in four row groups, blocks of consecutive rows, and its footer, a summary at the end of the file, records their ranges as 1 to 250, 251 to 500, 501 to 750 and 751 to 1000. A query asks for the row with `order_id = 600`. How much of the file does the reader have to open?
hints: The footer gives each group's smallest and largest `order_id`.
Which ranges could contain 600?

acceptedIdeas: Only the row group whose range includes 600
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only the row group whose range includes 600

questions.onCorrect: The other three groups are skipped using nothing but the ranges, without a single data value being read.

misconceptions.feedback: The footer already says that three of the groups hold no value near 600, since 600 lies outside their ranges, so the reader has no reason to open them.
The ranges do not overlap, so only one group can contain 600. A neighbouring group whose range ends at 500 or starts at 751 cannot hold it.

choices.label: Two row groups, the one whose range includes 600 and the one beside it
Only the row group whose range includes 600
All four row groups, because any of them might hold the row

questions.prompt: Row groups have `order_id` ranges 1 to 120, 100 to 260, 240 to 400 and 390 to 520. A query filters `order_id = 250`. How many row groups must be read?
hints: Test 250 against each range in turn.
A range includes both of its end values.
Count the ranges that include 250.
questions.onCorrect: Overlapping ranges mean more groups could hold the value, so fewer can be skipped.

misconceptions.feedback: Ranges that overlap can both include 250. Check 100 to 260 and 240 to 400.
Two of the four ranges exclude 250, and those groups can be skipped.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 250 lies in 100 to 260 and in 240 to 400, so both groups could hold it. The ranges 1 to 120 and 390 to 520 exclude it, so 2 groups are read.

questions.prompt: Complete the working: how many gigabytes (10^9 bytes) does the columnar reader fetch for 3 columns of 200,000,000 values of 4 bytes?
hints: Multiply the rows by the 3 columns.
Then multiply by the 4 bytes of each value.
Divide by 1,000,000,000 to give gigabytes.
questions.onCorrect: The result is a quarter of the row layout's 9.6 GB, matching the 3 of 12 columns the query needs.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the row layout, which passes over all 12 columns.
That is the size of one column of 4 bytes. The query needs three.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 200,000,000 × 3 × 4 = 2,400,000,000 bytes, which is 2.4 GB and a quarter of the 9.6 GB the row layout reads.

questions.prompt: An account page loads one customer's whole profile, all 40 columns of it, by customer id each time someone signs in, thousands of times a second. Which file layout suits it?
hints: The service needs every column, but only of one row.
Ask where the values of one record sit in each layout.

acceptedIdeas: Row-oriented, because one complete record sits in one contiguous run of bytes
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Row-oriented, because one complete record sits in one contiguous run of bytes

questions.onCorrect: A row layout keeps each record's values together, so one contiguous read returns the whole order.

misconceptions.feedback: A columnar file saves bytes when a query reads a few columns of many rows. Fetching every column of one row means visiting a separate place for each column and then putting the record back together.
At thousands of lookups a second the cost of each lookup adds up, and a columnar reader makes one visit per column where a row reader makes one in all.

choices.label: Columnar, because it reads only the columns a query needs
Either, because a single record is too small for the layout to matter
Row-oriented, because one complete record sits in one contiguous run of bytes

questions.prompt: A columnar file has 10,000,000 rows of 30 columns of 8 bytes. A query needs 4 columns, and compression stores them at a quarter of their raw size. How many megabytes (10^6 bytes) does the reader fetch?
hints: Work out the raw bytes of the 4 columns first.
10,000,000 × 4 × 8 gives bytes.
Then take a quarter of the result.
questions.onCorrect: The 4 of 30 columns and the quartering by compression combine, so the reader fetches a small part of the table's raw size.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the raw size of the 4 columns. Compression stores them at a quarter of it.
That is all 30 columns, before compression and before choosing only 4 columns.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Raw size of 4 columns is 10,000,000 × 4 × 8 = 320,000,000 bytes, or 320 MB. A quarter of that is 80 MB.

questions.prompt: A row-oriented file of 40,000,000 rows and 25 eight-byte columns must be read in full, although the query needs only 2 columns. How many gigabytes (10^9 bytes) are read?
hints: A row layout cannot read just two columns.
Multiply rows, columns and bytes per value.
Convert bytes to gigabytes by dividing by 10^9.
questions.onCorrect: A row layout reads every column, so the 2 needed columns save nothing and the whole 8 GB is fetched.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what a columnar file would read for 2 columns. A row layout reads all 25.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: All 25 columns are read: 40,000,000 × 25 × 8 = 8,000,000,000 bytes, or 8 GB.

questions.prompt: A Parquet row group's `order_id` column has a minimum of 1 and a maximum of 300 in the file's footer. A query filters `order_id = 500`. What does the reader do with that row group?
hints: Compare 500 with the group's minimum and maximum.

acceptedIdeas: Skips it, because 500 lies outside the range 1 to 300
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Skips it, because 500 lies outside the range 1 to 300

questions.onCorrect: 500 lies above the maximum of 300, so the group cannot hold it and the reader skips it using the footer alone.

misconceptions.feedback: A range is enough to rule a group out: no value in it can be larger than the maximum, so 500 cannot be there.
The footer's maximum of 300 already settles the question, so the reader need not open any chunk of this group.

choices.label: Skips it, because 500 lies outside the range 1 to 300
Reads only its `order_id` chunk, to check for 500
Reads it in full, because the footer gives only a range

questions.prompt: Which format best suits repeated analytical queries that read a few columns of billions of rows?
hints: Look for a columnar format that records min and max statistics.
Row formats read every column.
questions.onCorrect: Parquet stores columns together with a footer of statistics, so a query reads only the columns and row groups it needs.

misconceptions.feedback: Avro is row-oriented and suits messages sent record by record, so a column query would read every column.
CSV is row-oriented text with no types, and a query must read all of it.
JSON lines is row-oriented text, so every field of every line has to be read.

choices.label: CSV
Avro
Parquet
JSON lines

questions.prompt: A source of 10,000,000 rows has 25,000 rows change each day. An incremental load runs every night. How many rows does it move in 7 nights?
hints: How many rows move on one night?
The size of the whole source does not matter to an incremental load.
Multiply one night's rows by 7.
questions.onCorrect: An incremental load pays only for the rows that changed, so its cost follows the changes and not the size of the table.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what 7 full loads would move. An incremental load moves only the changed rows.
That is a single night. The question asks for 7.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each night moves the 25,000 rows that changed, and 7 × 25,000 = 175,000 rows.

questions.prompt: A customers table has 3 rows, with ids 1, 2 and 3, and no key declared. A batch of 2 rows, with ids 2 and 4, is added with a plain `INSERT`, and the scheduler runs the job twice because the first run seemed to time out. What does the table hold afterwards?
hints: The table has no key, so nothing stops a repeated id.
Count what each run adds to the 3 rows already there.

acceptedIdeas: 7 rows, with id 2 three times and id 4 twice
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 7 rows, with id 2 three times and id 4 twice

questions.onCorrect: Without a key to compare, each run adds its rows again, so 7 rows hold only 4 distinct customers.

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing merges rows by `id` unless the table declares `id` as a key and the write says what to do on a clash. A plain `INSERT` adds every row it is given.
The second run adds the same 2 rows again, since a plain `INSERT` does not look at what the table already holds.

choices.label: 5 rows, because the second run adds nothing new
4 rows, ids 1 to 4, because rows with the same id are merged
7 rows, with id 2 three times and id 4 twice

questions.prompt: A customers table has 3 rows (ids 1, 2, 3). A 2-row batch (ids 2 and 4) is written as an upsert keyed on id, and the job is run twice. How many rows does the table hold?
hints: Which ids in the batch already exist?
An existing key is updated, not added.
Count the distinct ids after the batch.
questions.onCorrect: The table holds one row per distinct id, whether the batch runs once or ten times.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the plain `INSERT` answer. An upsert updates a row whose key already exists.
That adds both batch rows as new. Id 2 already exists and is updated in place.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Id 2 already exists and is updated, and id 4 is new and is added, giving 4 rows. The second run finds both keys and changes nothing.

questions.prompt: The watermark is 11:30 and the source rows have `updated_at` 11:20, 11:30, 11:45 and 12:05. How many rows does `WHERE updated_at > '11:30'` select?
hints: Which values are later than 11:30?
The row at exactly 11:30 is not strictly greater.
Count the values after 11:30.
questions.onCorrect: Strictly greater than excludes the row stamped exactly at the watermark, so a tie is never read again.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count for greater than or equal, which keeps the row at 11:30.
Both 11:45 and 12:05 are later than 11:30.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only 11:45 and 12:05 are strictly later than 11:30, so 2 rows are selected.

questions.prompt: What does the watermark become after this run? Give it as hh:mm.
hints: The watermark is the largest `updated_at` among the rows just loaded.
Which of the two loaded rows is later?
questions.onCorrect: The watermark is taken from the data that was loaded, and 10:09 is the latest change it contains.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the first loaded row. The watermark moves to the largest `updated_at` loaded.

questions.prompt: Source rows are stamped 05-01 (1 row), 05-02 (2 rows), 05-03 (3 rows) and 05-04 (1 row), and `updated_at` is a date. A run reads everything from 05-01 onwards, inclusive. How many rows does it read?
hints: Which days does the run include?
The run starts on 05-01 and includes it.
Add the rows of each day.
questions.onCorrect: The overlap re-reads rows already loaded, and an upsert absorbs them, which is why the two techniques go together.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the strict filter after 05-03. The overlap starts at 05-01.
That leaves out one day. The run includes 05-01 itself.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: From 05-01 onwards includes every day: 1 + 2 + 3 + 1 = 7 rows.

questions.prompt: A table holds 5 rows with ids 1 to 5. A batch of 3 rows with ids 4, 5 and 6 is written as an upsert keyed on id, and the job is run 3 times. How many rows does the table hold?
hints: Which ids in the batch already exist?
Only one id in the batch is new.
Repeating the job adds nothing further.
questions.onCorrect: An upsert leaves one row per distinct id, so extra runs of the same batch do not change the count.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count if every run inserted all 3 rows. An upsert updates rows whose ids exist.
That adds the batch once as new rows, but ids 4 and 5 already exist.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Ids 4 and 5 already exist and are updated, and id 6 is added, so the table holds ids 1 to 6, which is 6 rows, however many times the job runs.

questions.prompt: The stored watermark is 09:30. The source has rows updated at 09:15, 09:30, 09:30, 09:45 and 10:00. How many rows does `WHERE updated_at >= '09:30'` select?
hints: Does the comparison include the watermark itself?
Cross out the row at 09:15.
Count what is left.
questions.onCorrect: Greater than or equal re-reads rows stamped at the watermark, which an upsert can absorb safely.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count for strictly greater than. The comparison here includes the rows at 09:30.
The row at 09:15 is earlier than the watermark and is not selected.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The two rows at 09:30 pass because the comparison includes equality, and so do 09:45 and 10:00. That makes 4 rows.

questions.prompt: Which statement can be run twice without changing the result of the first run?
hints: Look for the statement that finds an existing row by its key.
A statement that builds on the current value changes it each time.
questions.onCorrect: The `ON CONFLICT` clause turns a repeated insert into an update with identical values, so a second run changes nothing.

misconceptions.feedback: A plain `INSERT` adds the row again on every run, or fails once a key exists.
This multiplies the current price each time, so every run changes it further.
A row with no id is added as a new row on every run.

choices.label: `INSERT INTO products VALUES (5, 'tape', 2.20) ON CONFLICT(id) DO UPDATE SET price = excluded.price;`
`INSERT INTO products VALUES (5, 'tape', 2.20);`
`INSERT INTO products VALUES (NULL, 'tape', 2.20);`
`UPDATE products SET price = price * 1.1;`

acceptedIdeas: `INSERT INTO products VALUES (5, 'tape', 2.20) ON CONFLICT(id) DO UPDATE SET price = excluded.price;`
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: INSERT INTO products VALUES (5, 'tape', 2.20) ON CONFLICT(id) DO UPDATE SET price = excluded.price;

questions.prompt: A source and its warehouse copy each hold 5 rows. One source row is hard-deleted, and a nightly job upserts the rows with `updated_at` beyond its watermark into the copy. How many rows does the copy hold afterwards?
hints: Can the query select a row that no longer exists?
What does an upsert do to rows it is not given?
Nothing removes a row from the copy.
questions.onCorrect: An upsert adds and updates rows but never removes them, so a delete at the source stays invisible without the log.

misconceptions.feedback: That would need the job to learn about the delete, and a timestamp filter cannot see a row that no longer exists.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The deleted row leaves nothing for the timestamp filter to select, and an upsert only inserts or updates, so all 5 rows remain in the copy.

questions.prompt: Apply to an empty table: `1 insert id 1 'x'; 2 insert id 2 'y'; 3 update id 1 'x2'; 4 delete id 2; 5 insert id 3 'z'`. How many rows does the table hold at the end?
hints: Track the set of ids after each entry.
An update changes a row but does not add one.
A delete removes a row.
questions.onCorrect: Inserts add rows, updates change them and deletes remove them, so the final count is inserts minus deletes here.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts every entry as a row. An update changes an existing row and a delete removes one.
That counts the inserts only. One of those rows was deleted later.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Entries 1 and 2 add two rows, entry 3 changes id 1, entry 4 removes id 2, and entry 5 adds id 3, leaving ids 1 and 3, which is 2 rows.

questions.prompt: Three entries come from a source's change log: position 1 inserts id 1 with value 'a', position 2 deletes id 1, and position 3 inserts id 1 with value 'b'. They reach the warehouse in the order 1, 3, 2, and the warehouse applies them in the order they arrive. What does the warehouse table hold at the end?
hints: Apply the entries one at a time in the order 1, 3, 2.
Ask what the delete finds when it is applied last.

acceptedIdeas: No rows, because the delete is applied last
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No rows, because the delete is applied last

questions.onCorrect: Applied in the log's own order the table would hold 1 row, so the arrival order has lost a row.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the source's result, reached by applying the entries in the order 1, 2, 3. Here the delete arrives after the second insert and removes the row it wrote.
The second insert of id 1 arrives while the first row is still there, and the delete that follows removes the row with that key, so nothing is left.

choices.label: Two rows with id 1, one holding 'a' and one holding 'b'
One row, id 1 with value 'b', the same as the source
No rows, because the delete is applied last

questions.prompt: What value does id 4 hold when the log ends?
hints: Entry 6 is the last change to id 4.
An update replaces the value of the row with that key.
questions.onCorrect: The last entry for a key decides its value, and an earlier insert or update is overwritten.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the value after entry 5. Entry 6 then updates id 4.

questions.prompt: A warehouse holds ids 1 to 8. The source now holds ids 1, 2, 4, 5, 7 and 8. How many warehouse rows should be deleted, by comparing keys?
hints: Which ids are missing from the source's list?
Check each id from 1 to 8 against the source's list.
Count the missing ids.
questions.onCorrect: A key present in the warehouse and absent from the source has been deleted, so comparing keys finds deletes that timestamps cannot.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of ids still in the source. The question asks for the ids to delete.
That is the warehouse's row count. Only the ids missing from the source are deleted.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Ids 3 and 6 appear in the warehouse but not in the source, so they were deleted at the source and 2 rows should be removed.

questions.prompt: A log applied to an empty table holds 5 inserts of different keys, 4 updates of existing rows and 2 deletes of existing rows. How many rows does the table hold at the end?
hints: Which operations change the number of rows?
An update changes values in a row that is already there.
Subtract the deletes from the inserts.
questions.onCorrect: Only inserts and deletes move the row count, and updates leave it unchanged.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts every entry as a row. Updates and deletes do not add rows.
That counts only the inserts. The 2 deletes removed rows.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each insert adds a row, each delete removes one, and updates change no count, so 5 − 2 = 3 rows.

questions.prompt: Apply this log in position order to an empty table: `1 I id1 'a'; 2 I id2 'b'; 3 U id1 'a2'; 4 D id2; 5 I id3 'c'; 6 U id3 'c2'; 7 U id1 'a3'; 8 I id2 'b-new'`. What value does `id1` hold at the end? Give the value only.
hints: Look for the last entry that touches id1.
Entries 3 and 7 both update id1.
questions.onCorrect: The last entry for id1 is the update at position 7, so id1 holds a3, whatever it held before.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the value after entry 3. Entry 7 updates id1 again.
That is the value after the insert. Entries 3 and 7 update it later.

questions.prompt: The same log applied in position order: `1 I id1 'a'; 2 I id2 'b'; 3 U id1 'a2'; 4 D id2; 5 I id3 'c'; 6 U id3 'c2'; 7 U id1 'a3'; 8 I id2 'b-new'`. How many rows does the table hold at the end?
hints: Track which ids exist after each entry.
Id 2 is deleted at position 4.
Id 2 is inserted again at position 8.
questions.onCorrect: Position 8 inserts id 2 again after its delete, so a log can bring a key back and the order decides the outcome.

misconceptions.feedback: That forgets that the last entry inserts id 2 again after its delete.
That counts every entry as a row. Updates and the delete change no row count the way inserts do.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Ids 1, 3 and 2 exist at the end: id 2 was deleted at position 4 and inserted again at position 8, so the table holds 3 rows.

questions.prompt: Why does a nightly `WHERE updated_at > watermark` query not reflect rows hard-deleted at the source?
hints: Think about what a hard delete leaves behind in the source table.
The filter can only return rows that exist.
questions.onCorrect: A hard delete removes the row and its timestamp together, so a timestamp filter has nothing to return.

misconceptions.feedback: A time zone error would shift which rows are selected, but it would not hide a row that has been removed.
A query on the table has no way to see the delete, on the first night or later.
An upsert never removes rows at all. The limit is that no row exists to select.

choices.label: A deleted row no longer exists to carry a timestamp.
Deletes are always applied the next day.
Upserts refuse to remove rows with a timestamp.
The watermark is stored in the wrong time zone.

acceptedIdeas: A deleted row no longer exists to carry a timestamp.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A deleted row no longer exists to carry a timestamp.

questions.prompt: Three source tasks can run in any order, then the join, then the publish task. Only one task runs at a time. How many different orders can the five tasks run in?
hints: The join and publish step have only one possible position each.
How many ways can three sources be put in a row?
Choose the first source in 3 ways, the second in 2, the third in 1.
questions.onCorrect: Only the tasks without an arrow between them can swap places, so the arrows cut down the number of valid orders.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the choices for the first source only. Each choice leaves 2 for the next position.
That counts every task as free to move, but the join and publish tasks have fixed places.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The sources can be arranged in 3 × 2 × 1 = 6 ways, and the join and the publish step then follow in their only order, so there are 6 orders.

questions.prompt: Task X (3 min) feeds Y (5 min) and Z (8 min), and W (2 min) reads both Y and Z. With unlimited workers, what is the minimum total time in minutes?
hints: Y and Z can run at the same time.
W cannot start until both Y and Z have finished.
Add the tasks along the longer branch.
questions.onCorrect: Y and Z overlap, so only the longer one counts toward the total, and the shorter one has slack.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds every task, which is the time with a single worker. Y and Z can overlap.
That follows the shorter branch through Y. W must wait for Z as well.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Y and Z run side by side, and W waits for the slower one, so the longest chain is X, Z, W: 3 + 8 + 2 = 13 minutes.

questions.prompt: A failing task is retried 3 times, with waits of 2, 4 and 8 minutes before the retries. If every retry fails, how many minutes are spent waiting in total?
hints: How many waits are there?
List the three waits.
Add them.
questions.onCorrect: The waits double each time, so the last wait is as long as the other two together plus 2 minutes.

misconceptions.feedback: That is only the last wait. All three waits are spent before the final retry.
That adds only the first two waits. The retry after the third wait is also delayed by it.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The waits add up: 2 + 4 + 8 = 14 minutes.

questions.prompt: A task fails and the scheduler retries it 3 times, waiting 2 minutes before the first retry and doubling the wait before each retry after that. Every retry fails too. How does the total time spent waiting compare with retrying after a fixed wait of 2 minutes each time?
hints: Write down the three waits when each one doubles the last.
Three fixed waits of 2 minutes come to 6 minutes.

acceptedIdeas: More than twice as long, because the later waits grow quickly
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: More than twice as long, because the later waits grow quickly

questions.onCorrect: The doubling waits are 2, 4 and 8 minutes, 14 in all, against 6 minutes for three fixed waits of 2.

misconceptions.feedback: Only the first wait is the same. Each later wait is double the one before, so the second and third waits are far longer than 2 minutes.
Doubling adds up faster than that: the waits become 2, 4 and 8 minutes, which is 14 minutes against 6 for three fixed waits.

choices.label: A little longer, by a minute or two
More than twice as long, because the later waits grow quickly
About the same, since the first wait is 2 minutes in both cases

questions.prompt: A task takes 5 minutes to fail. It is attempted once and retried 3 times with waits of 2, 4 and 8 minutes, and every attempt fails. How many minutes pass from the first start until the last attempt fails?
hints: How many attempts are there in all?
Add the time of the attempts and the time of the waits.
Four attempts of 5 minutes, plus waits of 2, 4 and 8.
questions.onCorrect: A task that keeps failing delays everything after it for the attempts and the waits together.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the waiting time only. The four attempts take time as well.
That is the four attempts without the waits between them.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: There are 4 attempts of 5 minutes, which is 20 minutes, and 14 minutes of waits, so 34 minutes pass in all.

questions.prompt: How many minutes does the backfill take, with 8 waves of 10 minutes each?
hints: Each wave lasts as long as one run.
Multiply the number of waves by the minutes in a wave.
Use 8 waves, not 7.5.
questions.onCorrect: The backfill lasts one run for every wave, and rounding the waves up counts the partly filled last one.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses 7.5 waves. A partly filled wave still takes as long as a full one.
That runs all 45 partitions in turn, ignoring that 6 run at the same time.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: There are 8 waves and each lasts 10 minutes, so the backfill takes 8 × 10 = 80 minutes.

questions.prompt: A backfill of 20 daily partitions has runs of 10 minutes, and the limit is raised from 3 to 5 at a time. How many minutes does it take now?
hints: Divide the partitions by 5.
Check whether the last wave is full.
Multiply the waves by 10 minutes.
questions.onCorrect: Raising the limit shortens the backfill because fewer waves are needed, until the source or the cluster becomes the bottleneck.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the time at the old limit of 3 at a time.
That is a single wave. At 5 at a time the partitions need 4 waves.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 20 ÷ 5 = 4 waves, with no part wave left over, and 4 × 10 = 40 minutes.

questions.prompt: Task A (5 min) feeds B (10 min) and C (4 min). B and C both feed D (6 min). D feeds E (2 min). With unlimited workers, what is the minimum total time in minutes?
hints: Find the longer of the two branches between A and D.
B and C run side by side, so the slower one counts.
Add A, the slower branch, D and E.
questions.onCorrect: C runs alongside B and finishes sooner, so its time never reaches the total, which B, D and E set.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds every task, which is the time with a single worker.
That goes through C, the shorter branch. D has to wait for B as well.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The longest chain is A, B, D, E: 5 + 10 + 6 + 2 = 23 minutes. C runs beside B and has slack.

questions.prompt: In the same graph, A feeds B and C, both feed D, and D feeds E. How many different valid run orders does it have, if one task runs at a time?
hints: Which tasks have a fixed place?
Only B and C are free to change places.
B before C, or C before B.
questions.onCorrect: Only tasks with no arrow between them can swap, and here that is just the pair B and C.

misconceptions.feedback: B and C have no arrow between them, so either can go first.
That treats 3 tasks as free. A comes first and D and E follow, so only B and C can swap.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A must come first and E last, with D before E. B and C can swap, so the orders are A B C D E and A C B D E: 2 orders.

questions.prompt: A backfill must run 30 daily partitions, 4 at a time, each taking 12 minutes. How many minutes does it take if each batch of 4 starts when the previous one ends?
hints: Divide the partitions by the number at a time and round up.
The last, partly filled wave still takes a whole run.
