Multiply the waves by 12 minutes.
questions.onCorrect: The last wave holds only 2 partitions but lasts as long as a full one, so 8 waves are paid for.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses 7 waves. The last 2 partitions need an eighth wave.
That runs all 30 in turn, which ignores that 4 run at the same time.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 30 ÷ 4 = 7.5, which rounds up to 8 waves, and 8 × 12 = 96 minutes.

questions.prompt: A file holds 10,000 rows and 120 have text in a numeric column. A schema-on-write system refuses the faulty rows at load. How many rows does it load?
hints: Which rows does the schema check refuse?
Subtract the faulty rows from the total.
questions.onCorrect: Schema-on-write keeps faulty rows out of the table at load time, so later readers never meet them.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what a schema-on-read lake would accept. A schema-on-write system refuses the faulty rows.
That is the number of refused rows. The question asks how many are loaded.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The 120 faulty rows are refused, so 10,000 − 120 = 9,880 rows are loaded.

questions.prompt: Three engines, a SQL engine, a Spark engine and a machine-learning engine, each keep their own 2 TB copy of the same table, 6 TB in all. Roughly how much of that storage would be saved if all three could read one shared copy instead?
hints: How many 2 TB copies are left when all three engines share one?
questions.onCorrect: Sharing a copy also removes the risk that separate copies drift apart and give different answers.

misconceptions.feedback: An engine needs its own copy only when it cannot read the others' files. If the files are open and shared, one copy serves all three.
One shared copy keeps a single 2 TB table, so two of the three copies disappear and only a third of the storage remains.

choices.label: None, because each engine still needs its own copy
About a third of it
About two thirds of it

questions.prompt: Bronze holds 2,000 events, of which 250 are repeats of earlier events. Silver keeps one row per event. How many rows does silver hold?
hints: Does silver keep the repeats?
Subtract the repeats from bronze.
questions.onCorrect: Silver is where duplicates are removed, while bronze keeps every row exactly as it arrived.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the bronze count. Silver removes the repeats.
That is the number of repeats. Silver keeps the rest.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Silver drops the repeats, so 2,000 − 250 = 1,750 rows remain.

questions.prompt: Which layer holds ready-made tables built for one use, such as monthly revenue? Give the layer's name.
hints: Bronze is raw and silver is cleaned. Which layer comes after silver?
The layer closest to the readers who want finished numbers.
questions.onCorrect: Gold tables are built for a use from silver, so readers get totals without repeating the cleaning.

misconceptions.feedback: Silver holds cleaned rows of the events themselves. A monthly total built for one use is the next layer.

questions.prompt: A bug in last month's cleaning has been fixed, and the team must rebuild the cleaned tables from the events exactly as they arrived. Which medallion layer do they read from?
hints: Which layer is only ever added to and never changed?
Ask how far each layer has moved from the files as they arrived.
questions.onCorrect: Bronze keeps what arrived unchanged, so any later layer can be rebuilt from it if the cleaning was wrong.

misconceptions.feedback: Silver holds cleaned rows, with types fixed and duplicates removed, so it is no longer the data exactly as it arrived.
Gold holds tables built from silver for particular uses, such as totals, which are even further from the files as they arrived.

choices.label: Bronze
Silver
Gold

questions.prompt: A gold table holds one row per day per region, for 30 days and 4 regions. How many rows does it hold?
hints: Count the combinations of day and region.
Each day has 4 rows.
Multiply days by regions.
questions.onCorrect: Gold is much smaller than silver because it holds totals, which is why dashboards read it quickly.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the days and the regions. Each day has a row for every region, so they multiply.
That is one row per day. Each day has a row for each of the 4 regions.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Every day has one row for each region, so 30 × 4 = 120 rows.

questions.prompt: A table holds one cleaned row per customer, with types fixed and duplicates removed. Which medallion layer is it?
hints: Ask whether the table has been changed from what arrived, and whether it was built for one particular use.
questions.onCorrect: Silver holds cleaned rows at the grain of the events or entities, ready to feed gold tables.

misconceptions.feedback: Bronze keeps data exactly as it arrived, duplicates and faulty types included, so a cleaned table has already left it.
Gold holds tables built for one use, such as revenue per month. A cleaned table of customers is general-purpose detail that gold tables are built from.

choices.label: Gold
Bronze
Silver

questions.prompt: Several engines, a SQL engine and a Spark engine, must read the same single copy of the data with transactions. Which architecture fits?
hints: Look for open files with a table format on top.
One copy, several engines, and transactions.
questions.onCorrect: A lakehouse keeps open files with a table format, so several engines share one transactional copy.

misconceptions.feedback: A warehouse that keeps data inside its own engine does not let a second engine read the same copy.
Plain CSV files give several engines one copy, but with no transactions or table format.
A copy per engine is exactly what sharing avoids, and the copies can drift apart.

choices.label: A warehouse that keeps data only inside its own engine
Lakehouse
A separate copy for each engine
A folder of CSV files with no table format

questions.prompt: Which system applies a schema when data is read rather than when it is written? Give the system's name.
hints: Think of the system that accepts files as they arrive.
The warehouse is the one that checks at load.
questions.onCorrect: A lake accepts files as they are and applies a schema at read time, so bad values surface in queries.

misconceptions.feedback: A warehouse applies its schema when rows are written, and refuses rows that do not fit.

questions.prompt: Version 0 adds x, y and z. Version 1 removes x and adds w. Version 2 removes y. How many files make up the table at version 2?
hints: Write down the live files after each version.
A removed file leaves the live set.
Count what remains at the last version.
questions.onCorrect: Each commit adds to and removes from the live set, so the table at a version is the result of replaying every commit up to it.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts every file ever added. Removed files leave the live set.
That is the count one commit too early. The last commit removes y.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: After version 0 the live files are x, y, z. Version 1 gives y, z, w, and version 2 gives z and w, so 2 files.

questions.prompt: The latest checkpoint is at version 30 and the latest commit is version 41. How many commit files must a reader apply after loading the checkpoint?
hints: Does the checkpoint include version 20 itself?
Count the versions after 30 up to 41.
41 minus 30.
questions.onCorrect: The checkpoint stands in for every commit up to its version, so only the later commits are read.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts version 30 as well, but the checkpoint already includes it.
That would replay the whole log. The checkpoint replaces versions 0 to 30.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The checkpoint already includes version 30, so the reader applies versions 31 to 41, which is 11 commit files.

questions.prompt: The latest version in a table's commit log is 4. Two writers both read version 4 and both try to create version 5 at the same moment, with changes that do not conflict. The storage layer lets only one of them create that file. What happens to the two changes?
hints: Only one writer can create the file for version 5.
Ask what stops the other writer from trying the next number.

acceptedIdeas: One change becomes version 5, and the other is tried again as version 6
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: One change becomes version 5, and the other is tried again as version 6

questions.onCorrect: Each writer's commit takes the next free version number, so the log stays a single ordered line.

misconceptions.feedback: The writer that failed has not lost its files, only the race for the name. Since its change does not conflict with the winner's, it can simply commit after it.
Version 5 is a single file created by a single writer, and the storage layer lets only one writer create it, so nothing merges the two into one commit.

choices.label: One change becomes version 5, and the other is tried again as version 6
Both changes are merged into a single version 5
One change becomes version 5 and the other is lost

questions.prompt: A query starts when the latest version of a table is 12. While it runs, writers commit versions 13 and 14. Which version does the query read?
hints: A query reads one snapshot from beginning to end.

acceptedIdeas: Version 12, the one it fixed when it started
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Version 12, the one it fixed when it started

questions.onCorrect: The query sees one consistent snapshot, so concurrent commits never produce a half-updated view.

misconceptions.feedback: A query fixes its version at the start and reads that snapshot throughout, so commits made while it runs do not reach it.
Mixing versions would give a table that never existed, with part of a commit's changes and not the rest. Reading one fixed snapshot is what prevents that.

choices.label: Version 12, the one it fixed when it started
Version 12 for the files it read early and version 14 for the rest
Version 14, the latest by the time it finishes

questions.prompt: A table has 8 live files. A compaction rewrites 5 of them into 1 new file in one commit. How many files are on storage afterwards, before any vacuum?
hints: Does a commit that removes files delete their bytes?
Add the new file to the files already on storage.
8 plus 1.
questions.onCorrect: Compaction shrinks the live count but grows storage until a vacuum deletes the removed files.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the live count: 3 untouched files plus the new one. The removed files remain on storage.
That is the number of files compaction left alone. Storage holds more than that.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The commit adds 1 file and marks 5 as removed without erasing them, so storage holds 8 + 1 = 9 files.

questions.prompt: Version 0 adds m and n. Version 1 adds o and p. Version 2 removes m and adds q. Version 3 removes n. How many files are live at version 3?
hints: Write the live set after version 2.
The last commit only removes one file.
Count what is left.
questions.onCorrect: The live set after each commit is the previous set with that commit's removals and additions applied.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count before the last commit, which removes n.
Three files remain: o, p and q.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: After version 2 the live files are n, o, p and q. Version 3 removes n, leaving o, p and q: 3 files.

questions.prompt: A vacuum has deleted every file that the current version of a table does not use. Can the table still be read as it was at an earlier version that needed some of those files?
hints: Reading an old version means opening the files it lists.

acceptedIdeas: No, because some of the files that version lists are gone
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, because some of the files that version lists are gone

questions.onCorrect: A version can be read only while its files exist, so a vacuum ends time travel for versions that needed the deleted files.

misconceptions.feedback: The log still lists the files, but a list is not the data. Reading the version means opening those files, and the vacuum has deleted some of them.
A checkpoint is also a list of files and holds no data of its own, so it cannot bring back files that the vacuum deleted.

choices.label: No, because some of the files that version lists are gone
Yes, as long as a checkpoint was written at that version
Yes, because the commit log still describes that version

questions.prompt: Commits: v0 adds a and b. v1 adds c. v2 removes a and adds d. v3 adds e and removes b. v4 removes c and d and adds f. How many data files make up the table at version 2?
hints: Replay v0, v1 and v2 only.
Version 2 removes a and adds d.
Count the live files after v2.
questions.onCorrect: Replaying the log up to version 2 gives b, c and d, and the later commits do not change that version.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count after v1 plus the added d. Version 2 also removes a.
Three files remain after version 2: b, c and d.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: After v0 the live files are a, b. v1 gives a, b, c. v2 removes a and adds d, leaving b, c, d: 3 files.

questions.prompt: Using the same commits, v0 to v4, how many data files exist on storage after v4 and before any vacuum?
hints: Which files were ever added?
A removed file stays on storage until a vacuum.
Count a, b, c, d, e and f.
questions.onCorrect: Only 2 of the 6 files are live at version 4, and the other 4 stay until a vacuum deletes them.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of live files at v4, e and f. The removed files are still on storage.
That counts the live files at v2, not the files ever written.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Files a, b, c, d, e and f were each written once and none has been vacuumed, so 6 files are on storage.

questions.prompt: In which order does an Iceberg reader follow the metadata, from the start of a read to the data?
hints: The read starts at the one place that names the current table.
Statistics about data files sit in the manifest.
questions.onCorrect: The pointer names the current metadata file, which leads to a manifest list, then to manifests, then to data files.

misconceptions.feedback: The catalog pointer comes first, because it says which metadata file is current.
The manifest list comes before the manifests it lists, and the data files come last.
That reverses the chain. A reader starts at the pointer and ends at the data.

choices.label: Metadata file, catalog pointer, manifest, manifest list, data files
Catalog pointer, metadata file, manifest list, manifest, data files
Data files, manifest, manifest list, metadata file, catalog pointer
Catalog pointer, manifest, metadata file, data files, manifest list

acceptedIdeas: Catalog pointer, metadata file, manifest list, manifest, data files
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Catalog pointer, metadata file, manifest list, manifest, data files

questions.prompt: A 1,200 GB table has twelve equal monthly partitions. A query filters on the month column for 2 months. How many gigabytes does it read?
hints: How big is one monthly partition?
How many partitions does the filter open?
Multiply the two.
questions.onCorrect: Pruning cuts the read to the partitions the filter names, here a sixth of the table.

misconceptions.feedback: That reads every partition. A filter on the partition column skips the others.
That is a single partition. The filter names two months.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each partition holds 1,200 ÷ 12 = 100 GB, and 2 partitions are opened, so the query reads 200 GB.

questions.prompt: A 1,200 GB table partitioned by month has twelve partitions of 100 GB. Suppose it is partitioned by customer id instead, and there are 3,000,000 customers with equal amounts of data. Roughly how large is one partition?
hints: Divide 1,200 GB by 3,000,000 roughly: a gigabyte is a million kilobytes.
questions.onCorrect: Splitting one table into millions of partitions leaves each one far too small to read efficiently.

misconceptions.feedback: The table is the same size but is now divided into 3,000,000 pieces in place of twelve, so each piece is far smaller than a month.
A few gigabytes per partition would need only a few hundred partitions. Dividing 1,200 GB among 3,000,000 customers leaves each with well under a megabyte.

choices.label: A few hundred kilobytes
A few gigabytes
About 100 GB, the same as a month

questions.prompt: A sales table of billions of rows is queried mostly for a range of days or weeks. It has an `order_date` column with about 1,095 distinct dates over three years and a `customer_id` column with about 3,000,000 values. Which is the better partition column?
hints: A good partition column is used in filters and has a modest number of values.
Compare each column's values with the 1,200 GB example: how big would each partition be?

acceptedIdeas: `order_date`, because queries filter on it and it has few enough values
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: order_date, because queries filter on it and it has few enough values

questions.onCorrect: `order_date` is both filtered on and of moderate cardinality, so each partition stays large and pruning works.

misconceptions.feedback: Queries filter on dates, not customers, so partitions by customer would rarely be pruned, and 3,000,000 values would make each partition tiny.
Large tables are where partitioning pays most, as long as the column is one that queries filter on and its values are few enough to keep each partition large.

choices.label: `order_date`, because queries filter on it and it has few enough values
Neither, because a table this large should not be partitioned
`customer_id`, because it picks out rows most precisely

questions.prompt: A job writes one file every minute into each of 5 partitions. A day has 1,440 minutes. How many files does it create in one day?
hints: How many files does one partition get in a day?
There is one file per minute for each partition.
Multiply by the 5 partitions.
questions.onCorrect: Frequent small writes multiply quickly, which is why tables that are written often are compacted regularly.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the files for a single partition. There are 5 partitions.
The files are multiplied by the partitions, not added to them.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each partition receives 1,440 files, and 5 partitions give 5 × 1,440 = 7,200 files.

questions.prompt: Four files have `order_id` ranges 1 to 100, 50 to 150, 100 to 200 and 300 to 400. A query filters `order_id = 100`. How many files must be read?
hints: Check 100 against each range, including the end points.
A file can be skipped only if 100 lies outside its range.
Count the files that cannot be skipped.
questions.onCorrect: A range includes both of its end values, and overlapping ranges mean several files must be read for one value.

misconceptions.feedback: The ranges overlap, and 100 is inside more than one of them.
The range 300 to 400 does not include 100, so that file can be skipped.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first three ranges include 100, counting their end points, and only 300 to 400 does not, so 3 files are read.

questions.prompt: How many gigabytes does the query read, with 30 partitions of 5 GB each?
hints: Use the size of one partition from the first step.
Multiply by the 30 partitions opened.
30 times 5.
questions.onCorrect: A 30-day filter reads 30 of 360 partitions, about a twelfth of the table.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole table. Pruning leaves the other 330 partitions unread.
That is one partition. The query opens 30.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 30 partitions of 5 GB each give 30 × 5 = 150 GB, which is about 8.3% of the 1,800 GB table.

questions.prompt: A day's data is 7,200 files of 4 MB. Compaction rewrites it into files of about 200 MB. How many files hold the data afterwards?
hints: Work out the total data in megabytes first.
Divide the total by the target file size.
7,200 times 4, then divide by 200.
questions.onCorrect: Compaction keeps the same data in about a fiftieth as many files, so far fewer fixed costs are paid on each read.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of files before compaction.
That divides by 800 MB. The target file size is 200 MB.

questions.prompt: A 900 GB table has 360 equal daily partitions. A query filters 12 days. How many gigabytes does it read?
hints: How big is one daily partition?
How many partitions does the filter open?
Multiply them.
questions.onCorrect: Twelve days of 360 is a thirtieth of the partitions, so pruning reads a thirtieth of the table.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole table. The filter opens only 12 partitions.
That is one partition. The query opens 12.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each partition holds 900 ÷ 360 = 2.5 GB, and 12 days read 12 × 2.5 = 30 GB, which is a thirtieth of the table.

questions.prompt: 730 GB is partitioned by customer id across 2,000,000 customers, evenly. How many kilobytes (1 KB = 1,000 bytes) is one partition?
hints: Convert gigabytes to bytes.
Divide by the number of partitions.
Convert bytes to kilobytes.
questions.onCorrect: At 365 KB per partition, the cost of opening each folder and file outweighs the reading of its data.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the size in bytes. The question asks for kilobytes.
That is the size in megabytes. The question asks for kilobytes.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 730 GB is 730,000,000,000 bytes, and dividing by 2,000,000 gives 365,000 bytes, which is 365 KB.

questions.prompt: Files cover `order_id` ranges F1 1 to 300, F2 250 to 600, F3 601 to 900 and F4 400 to 700. A filter `order_id = 500` can skip how many of the four files?
hints: Test 500 against each file's range.
Which ranges include 500?
Count the files that do not.
questions.onCorrect: F2 and F4 overlap, so the filter on 500 cannot skip either of them, and only F1 and F3 are skipped.

misconceptions.feedback: That assumes only one file could hold 500. F2 and F4 both include it.
F1 ends at 300 and F3 starts at 601, so neither can hold 500.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 500 is inside F2 (250 to 600) and F4 (400 to 700), so those two must be read, and F1 and F3 can be skipped: 2 files.

questions.prompt: An input of 6 GiB is read in splits of 128 MiB (1 GiB = 1,024 MiB). How many tasks does the first stage run?
hints: Convert the input to MiB first.
6 × 1,024 gives the size in MiB.
Divide by 128 MiB per split.
questions.onCorrect: Each 128 MiB split becomes one partition and one task, so the task count follows from the size.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the size in MiB. Divide it by 128 MiB to find the number of splits.
That is the size in GiB. Each task takes a 128 MiB split.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 6 GiB is 6 × 1,024 = 6,144 MiB, and 6,144 ÷ 128 = 48 splits, so there are 48 tasks.

questions.prompt: A stage has 100 equal tasks and the cluster has 24 cores. How many waves does the stage need?
hints: Divide the tasks by the cores.
The result is not a whole number.
A partly filled wave still takes a round, so round up.
questions.onCorrect: Four full waves run 96 tasks, and a fifth wave runs the last 4, so the fifth wave counts in full.

misconceptions.feedback: That rounds down. The last 4 tasks still need a wave of their own.
That is the number of cores. The question asks for rounds of tasks.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 100 ÷ 24 is about 4.17, and a partly filled wave still has to run, so rounding up gives 5 waves.

questions.prompt: 80 map tasks each write one block for every one of 200 reducing partitions. How many shuffle blocks are produced?
hints: How many blocks does one map task write?
Every reducing partition gets a block from every map task.
Multiply the map tasks by the reducing partitions.
questions.onCorrect: The block count grows with the product of the two task counts, which is why a shuffle with many small partitions is slow.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two counts. Each map task writes a block for every reducing partition, so they multiply.
That is the blocks from one map task. There are 80 of them.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Every map task writes a block for every reducing partition, so 80 × 200 = 16,000 blocks.

questions.prompt: 500 million rows are shuffled by key to 5 reducing tasks, each processing 1 million rows per second, so an even split would take 100 seconds. One key holds 70% of the rows, and every row of a key goes to the same task. How long does the stage take, compared with the even split?
hints: How many rows does the task with the hot key receive?
A stage finishes only when its slowest task finishes.

acceptedIdeas: Several times longer, because one task receives most of the rows
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Several times longer, because one task receives most of the rows

questions.onCorrect: The stage ends when its slowest task ends, so one overloaded key sets the time for all five reducers.

misconceptions.feedback: The work is not shared evenly: every row of the hot key goes to one task, so that task receives 70% of the rows while the other four share the rest.
One task receives 350 million rows, which at 1 million rows per second takes 350 seconds, and the stage cannot end before its slowest task does.

choices.label: About the same, since five tasks still share the work
A little longer, perhaps 120 seconds
Several times longer, because one task receives most of the rows

questions.prompt: How many seconds does the hot key's task need to process 400 million rows at 2 million rows per second?
hints: Divide the rows by the rate.
Rows divided by rows per second gives seconds.
400 million divided by 2 million.
questions.onCorrect: The stage takes four times as long as the even split of 50 seconds, because one task carries 40% of the rows and an even task would carry 10%.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the time for an even split of 100 million rows each. The hot task holds 400 million.
That would be all the rows on one task. The hot key holds 40%.
That is the hot task's rows in millions. At 2 million rows per second it needs half as many seconds.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 400 million ÷ 2 million per second = 200 seconds, which is also the length of the stage, against 50 seconds for an even split.

questions.prompt: A program reads a table and then calls `df.filter(...).select(...).count()`. Which call makes the engine start the work?
hints: Which of the calls asks for a result to be returned to the program?
questions.onCorrect: count is an action, so it triggers the whole plan, while filter and select only add steps to it.

misconceptions.feedback: A filter is a transformation, so calling it only adds a step to the plan and no data is read yet.
A select is a transformation like the filter before it, and it too only adds a step to the plan.

choices.label: count
select
filter

questions.prompt: A 40 MB table is broadcast to 8 executors. How many megabytes does the broadcast move across the network?
hints: How many copies are sent?
One copy of 40 MB goes to each executor.
Multiply by 8.
questions.onCorrect: The cost grows with the small table and the number of executors, and does not depend on the size of the large table.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one copy. Every executor receives its own.
That is the size of the large table in MB, which a broadcast join does not move.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each executor receives a full copy of 40 MB, so 8 × 40 = 320 MB are moved.

questions.prompt: An input of 10 GiB is read in 128 MiB splits (1 GiB = 1,024 MiB). How many tasks run in the first stage?
hints: Convert 10 GiB to MiB.
10 × 1,024 gives the size in MiB.
Divide by 128.
questions.onCorrect: Each split is one partition and one task, so the count follows from the input size and the split size.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the size in MiB. Divide by 128 MiB to count the splits.
That is the size in GiB. Each task takes a 128 MiB split.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 10 GiB is 10,240 MiB, and 10,240 ÷ 128 = 80 splits, so the first stage runs 80 tasks.

questions.prompt: 1,000 million rows are shuffled to 10 reducers, each processing 1 million rows per second. One key holds 60% of the rows and goes to a single task. How many seconds does the stage take?
hints: How many rows does the hot key's task get?
60% of 1,000 million rows.
Divide by 1 million rows per second.
questions.onCorrect: An even split would take 100 seconds, so the skew makes the stage six times slower with no extra data.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the time for an even split over 10 reducers. One key holds 60%.
That is the percentage, not the seconds.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The hot key's task gets 0.6 × 1,000 million = 600 million rows, which takes 600 seconds, and the stage ends when it does.

questions.prompt: Is grouping rows by a key and counting each group a narrow or a wide transformation?
hints: Can each partition produce the final count for a key without seeing the other partitions?

acceptedIdeas: Wide, because the rows for each key must meet in one task
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Wide, because the rows for each key must meet in one task

questions.onCorrect: A group by must bring all rows with a key together, so every output reads from every input, which is a shuffle.

misconceptions.feedback: Counting rows one at a time would be narrow, but a count per key needs every row of that key in the same place, and they start out spread over many partitions.
A count over the whole table is an action, while a count per key is a grouping step in the plan, and its rows have to be shuffled so that each key's rows meet.

choices.label: Neither, because counting is an action
Narrow, because each row is counted once
Wide, because the rows for each key must meet in one task

questions.prompt: A table has 500 rows, and 80 of them re-send an earlier event with the same values but a new `loaded_at`. How many rows does `SELECT DISTINCT *` return?
hints: `DISTINCT` compares every column of a row.
Do the re-sent rows match their originals in `loaded_at`?
Rows that differ in any column are all kept.
questions.onCorrect: `DISTINCT` removes only rows identical in every column, so a re-sent record with a new load time survives it.

misconceptions.feedback: That assumes `DISTINCT` ignores `loaded_at`. It compares every column, and the re-sent rows differ in that one.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: `DISTINCT` compares every column, and each re-sent row differs from its original in `loaded_at`, so none is removed and all 500 rows are returned.

questions.prompt: Rows for one key were loaded on 03-01, 03-02 and 03-05. With `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY id ORDER BY loaded_at DESC)`, what `rn` does the row loaded on 03-02 get?
hints: Which load is newest, and so first in the order?
`DESC` puts the newest row first.
Count along: newest, then the one before it.
questions.onCorrect: `DESC` gives the newest row the first number, so `rn = 1` selects the latest load for each key.

misconceptions.feedback: The newest row, loaded on 03-05, gets that number because the order is descending.
That is the oldest row, loaded on 03-01. The order runs from newest to oldest.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Newest first the order is 03-05, 03-02, 03-01, so the row loaded on 03-02 is the second and gets `rn = 2`.

questions.prompt: A day's bronze table has 450 rows for 400 distinct events, because 50 events were sent twice. Every event is worth 10, so the true revenue is 4,000. What does `SUM(amount)` over the table as it stands return?
hints: SUM adds every row in the table.
How many rows does the table hold?

acceptedIdeas: More than 4,000, because each repeated row is added again
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: More than 4,000, because each repeated row is added again

questions.onCorrect: The sum cannot tell which rows are repeats, so it counts each copy as a separate event.

misconceptions.feedback: SUM adds every row it is given and has no idea which rows describe the same event, so a copy counts as much as the original.
Nothing in a sum subtracts a repeated row. Each of the 450 rows adds its 10, copies included.

choices.label: More than 4,000, because each repeated row is added again
Less than 4,000, because the repeats cancel each other
Exactly 4,000, because the repeats are copies of the same events

questions.prompt: The sum over bronze is 4,500 and the true revenue is 4,000. By what percentage of the true revenue is the sum too high?
hints: Find how much the sum exceeds the true revenue.
Divide that excess by the true revenue.
Multiply the result by 100.
questions.onCorrect: The error is measured against the true figure, and it grows with the share of events that were sent twice.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by the inflated total. The excess is measured against the true revenue.
That is the excess in revenue. The question asks for a percentage.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The excess is 4,500 − 4,000 = 500, and 500 ÷ 4,000 = 0.125, which is 12.5% of the true revenue.

questions.prompt: After deduplication a table has 960 rows, and 14 fail the numeric check and go to the reject table. How many rows continue to silver?
hints: Which rows leave the main flow?
The rejects are kept elsewhere, not lost.
960 minus 14.
questions.onCorrect: Rows that pass continue, and the rejects are kept with their reasons, so the 14 can be counted and repaired.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves the failing rows in the main flow. The 14 go to the reject table.
That adds the rejects to the total. They are removed from the main flow.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The 14 failing rows are removed from the main flow and kept in the reject table, so 960 − 14 = 946 rows continue.

questions.prompt: What is the total of the three kept amounts?
hints: Use only the rows kept after deduplication.
Add 6, 4 and 9.
The old values for k1 and k2 are not included.
questions.onCorrect: Deduplicating first gives 19, and summing the raw rows would overstate the total by 9.

misconceptions.feedback: That sums all five rows. The older rows for k1 and k2 are duplicates and are not kept.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The latest amounts are 6, 4 and 9, which add up to 19, whereas summing all five rows would give 28.

questions.prompt: A query numbers event e1's rows with `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY event_id ORDER BY loaded_at ASC)`, by mistake, and keeps `rn = 1`. The event was loaded on 2026-03-01 and again on 2026-03-02. Which row does it keep?
hints: Ascending order puts the smallest value first.
Which row gets `rn = 1`?

acceptedIdeas: The row loaded on 2026-03-01, the earliest
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The row loaded on 2026-03-01, the earliest

questions.onCorrect: Ascending order numbers the oldest row first, so the query keeps the first load and discards the latest word of the source.

misconceptions.feedback: The latest row comes first only with `ORDER BY loaded_at DESC`. In ascending order the oldest row comes first and receives `rn = 1`.
Each row does get its own number, but the filter keeps only `rn = 1`, which is one row per event.

choices.label: The row loaded on 2026-03-02, the latest
Both rows, since each has its own rn
The row loaded on 2026-03-01, the earliest

hints: Keep one row per `event_id`: the one with the latest `loaded_at`.
e3's latest row is the one loaded on 2026-03-02.
questions.onCorrect: Keeping the latest row per event drops the padded copy of e1 and the unusable x, so only four rows count.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds every row, repeats and the unusable value included. Keep only the latest row per event.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The latest rows are e1 10.5, e2 7, e3 4 and e4 5, which add up to 26.5.

questions.prompt: With the same six rows, what is `SUM(CAST(TRIM(amount) AS REAL))` over all six rows, without deduplicating? In SQLite a cast of `x` gives 0.
hints: TRIM removes the padding in ' 10.50'.
The cast of x gives 0.
Add all six converted values.
questions.onCorrect: The figure is 10.5 too high, because e1 is counted twice, and the quiet 0 for x hides a bad value.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the total after deduplication. Here every row is added, repeats included.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: All six rows count: 10.5 + 10.5 + 7 + 0 + 4 + 5 = 37.0, so the figure overstates the deduplicated total.

questions.prompt: Which step must come first, deduplication or aggregation?
hints: Can a total be corrected once the copies are inside it?

acceptedIdeas: Deduplication, so that no total counts a repeat
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Deduplication, so that no total counts a repeat

questions.onCorrect: Duplicated events would be counted more than once in a total, and the total cannot separate them afterwards.

misconceptions.feedback: Once rows are added together the copies can no longer be told apart, so a total taken first already includes them and cannot be corrected.
The totals differ whenever there are repeats: 450 rows give 4,500 and the 400 distinct events give 4,000.

choices.label: Aggregation, so that the copies can be counted
Deduplication, so that no total counts a repeat
Either, since the total comes out the same

questions.prompt: Event times are 09:02, 09:07, 09:11, 09:12, 09:19 and 09:21. With 10-minute tumbling windows starting at 09:00, how many events are in the window [09:10, 09:20)?
hints: The window includes 09:10 and excludes 09:20.
Which of the six times fall inside it?
Count them.
questions.onCorrect: A tumbling window includes its start and excludes its end, so each event falls in exactly one window.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the count for the window before it, [09:00, 09:10). The window from 09:10 holds 09:11, 09:12 and 09:19.
09:21 is after 09:20, so it belongs to the next window.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The events at 09:11, 09:12 and 09:19 are at least 09:10 and before 09:20, so the window holds 3 events.

questions.prompt: A 12-minute window slides every 4 minutes. In how many windows does each event fall?
hints: Windows start every 4 minutes.
How many starts fit inside one window length?
Divide the length by the step.
questions.onCorrect: The number of windows per event is the window length divided by the step, so a smaller step means more overlap.

misconceptions.feedback: That would be a tumbling window. A sliding window overlaps its neighbours.
That is the step in minutes. Divide the window length by it.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each event is covered by every window that starts within one window length before it, which is 12 ÷ 4 = 3 windows.

questions.prompt: Events occur at minutes 0, 2, 8, 9, 15, 16 and 30. Session windows close after a gap of 5 minutes without events. How many sessions are there?
hints: List the gaps between neighbouring events.
A gap of 5 or more ends a session.
Count the sessions, which is one more than the long gaps.
questions.onCorrect: Each long pause starts a new session, so the number of sessions is the number of long pauses plus one.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts every event as its own session. Events closer than the gap join one session.
That counts the long gaps. There is one more session than long gaps.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The sessions are {0, 2}, {8, 9}, {15, 16} and {30}, because the pauses 2 to 8, 9 to 15 and 16 to 30 are each at least 5 minutes: 4 sessions.

questions.prompt: A stream engine counts purchases per window, and it allows records to arrive up to 15 minutes late. The latest event time it has seen is 11:20. Up to what event time can it treat its windows as complete?
hints: A record can be up to 15 minutes behind the latest event time.
Which event times could a record still arriving carry?

acceptedIdeas: 11:05, fifteen minutes before the latest event time seen
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 11:05, fifteen minutes before the latest event time seen

questions.onCorrect: The watermark trails the latest event time by the allowed lateness, here 11:05, and it moves up only when later events arrive.

misconceptions.feedback: A record stamped 11:10 could still arrive, since it would be only 10 minutes behind the latest event, so windows up to 11:20 cannot be treated as complete yet.
Waiting is measured backwards from the latest event: a record may be up to 15 minutes behind 11:20, so the times still at risk run back to 11:05, not forward.

choices.label: 11:05, fifteen minutes before the latest event time seen
11:35, fifteen minutes after the latest event time seen
11:20, the latest event time it has seen

questions.prompt: The latest event time seen is 14:55 and the allowed lateness is 20 minutes. Has the window from 14:00 to 14:30 been closed?
hints: Work out the watermark: latest event time minus allowed lateness.
Compare it with the window's end.

acceptedIdeas: Yes, because the watermark of 14:35 is past the window's end
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes, because the watermark of 14:35 is past the window's end

questions.onCorrect: The watermark is 14:35, which is past the window's end at 14:30, so the engine no longer waits for records for it.

misconceptions.feedback: A record stamped 14:29 would now be 26 minutes behind the latest event, more than the 20 minutes allowed, so the engine no longer waits for it.
The engine can never know which record is the last, which is why it closes a window by the watermark and not by waiting for a final record.

choices.label: No, because a window closes only when its last record arrives
Yes, because the watermark of 14:35 is past the window's end
No, because a record stamped 14:29 could still arrive

questions.prompt: How many minutes is the event time 14:03 behind the watermark 14:31?
hints: Both times are in the same hour.
Subtract the minutes of 14:03 from the minutes of 14:31.
31 minus 3.
questions.onCorrect: The event is 28 minutes behind the watermark, and its window closed long before it arrived.

misconceptions.feedback: That subtracts from the latest event time 14:41. The question compares with the watermark.
That takes away the allowed lateness as well, but the gap to the watermark is the full difference.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: From 14:03 to 14:31 is 28 minutes, which is more than the 10 minutes of allowed lateness, so the event is too late to count.

questions.prompt: A consumer committed offset 300, then processed the records at offsets 300 to 306 and crashed before committing again. Which records does it process a second time after restarting?
hints: After a crash the consumer restarts from its last committed offset.

acceptedIdeas: The records at offsets 300 to 306, processed since the commit
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The records at offsets 300 to 306, processed since the commit

questions.onCorrect: Everything processed since the last commit is read again, so a sink that is not idempotent stores those records twice.

misconceptions.feedback: The commit marks where the consumer restarts, and it was made before offsets 300 to 306 were processed, so those records are read again.
The committed offset survives the crash, so the consumer restarts from 300 and not from the start of the log.

choices.label: The records at offsets 300 to 306, processed since the commit
Every record from offset 0, because the crash lost its place
None, because offset 300 was committed

questions.prompt: A purchase happened at 13:22 and arrived at 13:36. With 5-minute tumbling windows from 13:00, at what time does the window begin that holds it if windows follow arrival time? Give hh:mm.
hints: Arrival time is what decides the window here.
Which 5-minute window includes 13:36?
questions.onCorrect: Windows by arrival put the purchase at 13:35, a different window from the one it belongs to by event time.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the window by event time. With arrival time the purchase counts at 13:36.

questions.prompt: Events occur at 10:01, 10:04, 10:06, 10:09 and 10:10. With tumbling windows of 5 minutes starting at 10:00, how many events are in the window [10:05, 10:10)?
hints: The window includes 10:05 and excludes 10:10.
Which events lie inside it?
Count them.
questions.onCorrect: 10:10 starts the next window, since a window excludes its end, so the boundary event is counted there.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts 10:10, which is the start of the next window and not part of this one.
Both 10:06 and 10:09 are inside the window.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The events at 10:06 and 10:09 fall in that window. 10:10 belongs to the next window because the end is excluded: 2 events.

questions.prompt: The latest event time seen is 10:42 and the allowed lateness is 10 minutes. What is the watermark? Give it as hh:mm.
hints: Subtract the lateness from the latest event time.
10:42 minus 10 minutes.
questions.onCorrect: The watermark trails the latest event time by 10 minutes, so windows ending before 10:32 can be finalised.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the lateness. The watermark trails the latest event time.

questions.prompt: Events occur at minutes 0, 2, 3, 10, 12 and 20. Session windows close after a 5-minute gap with no events. How many sessions are there?
hints: List the gaps between neighbouring events.
A gap of 5 or more ends a session.
Count the groups.
questions.onCorrect: Two long pauses split the events into three sessions.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts every event as its own session. Events closer than the gap share one.
That counts the long pauses. There is one more session than long pauses.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The sessions are {0, 2, 3}, {10, 12} and {20}, because the pauses 3 to 10 and 12 to 20 are longer than 5 minutes: 3 sessions.

questions.prompt: A batch has 2,500 rows and 40 fail the not-null check. What percentage of the batch fails?
hints: Divide the failing rows by the rows in the batch.
40 divided by 2,500.
Multiply the result by 100 to get a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: The share of failing rows, and not the raw count, is what a threshold is compared with, since batches differ in size.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of failing rows. The question asks for a percentage of the batch.
That is the fraction. Multiply by 100 for a percentage.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 40 ÷ 2,500 = 0.016, which is 1.6% of the batch.

questions.prompt: A gate quarantines the 40 failing rows of a 2,500-row batch, because 1.6% is under its 2% threshold. How many rows continue to the next layer?
hints: Which rows leave the main flow?
The quarantined rows are kept elsewhere.
questions.onCorrect: Quarantine removes only the failing rows from the flow, and they stay in the quarantine table with their reasons.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves the failing rows in the flow. The gate sets them aside.
That is the quarantined rows. The question asks for the rows that continue.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The 40 failing rows are set aside and the rest go on: 2,500 − 40 = 2,460 rows.

questions.prompt: A source renames the column `cust` to `customer_id`, and nothing else changes. What happens to an existing downstream query that selects the column `cust`?
hints: Does the table still have a column with the name the query uses?

acceptedIdeas: It fails, because there is no longer a column called cust
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It fails, because there is no longer a column called cust

questions.onCorrect: The query names a column that no longer exists, so it fails with an error, which makes a rename a breaking change.

misconceptions.feedback: The query names `cust`, and nothing tells the database that `customer_id` is the same column under a new name, so it cannot find what the query asks for.
A column that is missing is not the same as a column of nulls. The database rejects a query that names a column the table does not have.

choices.label: It fails, because there is no longer a column called cust
It runs and returns cust as empty values
It runs and returns the same rows as before

questions.prompt: A source widens a text column from `VARCHAR(100)` to `VARCHAR(200)`, so every old value still fits. Is the change safe or breaking?
hints: Ask whether any query written against the old schema would fail or change its result.

acceptedIdeas: Safe, because every old query still gives the same answer
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Safe, because every old query still gives the same answer

questions.onCorrect: Every old value fits in the wider type, so existing queries give the same answers and the change is safe.

misconceptions.feedback: A change of type breaks a reader only when an old value no longer fits or an old query changes its answer. Every text of up to 100 characters also fits in 200, so neither happens.
Storage size does not change what a query returns. Every value and every result stays as it was.

choices.label: Breaking, because the column's type has changed
Safe, because every old query still gives the same answer
Breaking, because the column now takes twice the space

questions.prompt: A gate passes a batch if at most 2% of its rows fail. A batch has 4,000 rows. What is the greatest number of failing rows that still passes?
hints: Convert 2% to a fraction.
0.02 times the rows in the batch.
The limit itself is still allowed.
questions.onCorrect: The limit scales with the size of the batch, which is why the threshold is a percentage and not a fixed count.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the percentage. The question asks for a number of rows.
That takes 2% of 400. The batch has 4,000 rows.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 2% of 4,000 is 0.02 × 4,000 = 80, so a batch with up to 80 failing rows passes.

questions.prompt: What percentage of the 5,000 rows fail, when 110 rows fail?
hints: Divide the failing rows by the batch size.
110 divided by 5,000.
Multiply by 100 to give a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: 2.2% is over the 2% threshold, so the gate stops the run, although no single check failed on many rows.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of failing rows. The question asks for a percentage.
That is the fraction. Multiply by 100 for a percentage.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 110 ÷ 5,000 = 0.022, which is 2.2%, above the 2% threshold.

questions.prompt: The threshold is 5%. In a batch of 2,000 rows, 4% fail and are quarantined. How many rows continue?
hints: Is 4% over or under the 5% threshold?
Work out how many rows are 4% of 2,000.
Subtract them from the batch.
questions.onCorrect: Under the threshold the gate quarantines the failing rows and passes the rest, and the quarantine table keeps the 80.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves the failing rows in the flow. The gate sets them aside.
That is the number of quarantined rows. The question asks how many continue.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 4% of 2,000 is 80 failing rows, below the 5% limit, so 2,000 − 80 = 1,920 rows continue.

questions.prompt: Which source schema change is most likely to break downstream readers?
hints: Which change makes an existing query name something that is gone?
Safe changes leave old queries working.
questions.onCorrect: Renaming makes every query that names the old column fail, whereas additions and widening leave old queries working.

misconceptions.feedback: A nullable column that old queries never mention leaves them working.
Every old integer fits in the wider type, so old queries keep working.
A new table is not read by existing queries, so they are not affected.

choices.label: Adding a new table
Renaming a column
Adding a nullable column
Widening an integer column

questions.prompt: A batch has 1,000 rows and 30 fail the not-null check on the key. What percentage fails?
hints: Divide the failing rows by the batch size.
30 divided by 1,000.
Multiply by 100.
questions.onCorrect: The share is 3%, which is the figure to compare with a threshold.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of failing rows. The question asks for a percentage.
That is the fraction. Multiply by 100.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 30 ÷ 1,000 = 0.03, which is 3% of the batch.

questions.prompt: A gate has a 2% rejection threshold and 3% of the batch fails. What should the gate do?
hints: Compare 3% with the threshold.

acceptedIdeas: Stop the run and alert someone
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Stop the run and alert someone

questions.onCorrect: 3% is above the 2% limit, so the gate stops the run and alerts someone before bad data is published.

misconceptions.feedback: Quarantine is for a share of failures below the threshold. At 3%, above the 2% line, the failures suggest something upstream is broken and the batch as a whole should not be trusted.
The threshold exists so that a batch with this many failures is not published. Letting it through replaces yesterday's good data with today's doubtful data.

choices.label: Let the whole batch continue, since most rows passed
Quarantine the failing rows and let the rest continue
Stop the run and alert someone

questions.prompt: A table was last loaded at 04:25 and it is now 13:10. Its freshness target is 8 hours. How many minutes late is it?
hints: Work out the age of the table in hours and minutes.
Convert the age and the target to minutes.
Subtract the target from the age.
questions.onCorrect: Lateness is the age minus the target, and it counts only when the age exceeds the target.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the age in minutes. Subtract the 480-minute target to find how late it is.
That is the target in hours. The question asks how many minutes late the table is.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The age is 13:10 − 04:25 = 8 h 45 min, which is 525 minutes. The target is 480 minutes, so it is 45 minutes late.

questions.prompt: A job moves 252 million rows in 35 minutes. What is its throughput in rows per second?
hints: Convert the 35 minutes to seconds.
35 × 60 gives the seconds.
Divide the rows by the seconds.
questions.onCorrect: A rate in rows per second can be compared with the rate the deadline requires.

misconceptions.feedback: That is rows per minute. The question asks for rows per second.
That divides by 1,000 seconds. 35 minutes is 2,100 seconds.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 35 minutes is 2,100 seconds, and 252,000,000 ÷ 2,100 = 120,000 rows per second.

questions.prompt: A job usually writes 1,200,000 rows and tonight it wrote 600,000 and reported success. What percentage of the usual volume is that?
hints: Divide tonight's rows by the usual rows.
Multiply the fraction by 100.
questions.onCorrect: A run can succeed and still deliver half the data, which only a check on volume will reveal.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what the job's success status suggests. Half the usual rows were written.
That is the fraction. Multiply by 100 for a percentage.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 600,000 ÷ 1,200,000 = 0.5, which is 50% of the usual volume.

questions.prompt: A job usually writes 1,200,000 rows. Tonight it ran in its usual time and reported success, but it wrote only 600,000 rows. Which check would notice that something is wrong?
hints: Which number about tonight's run differs from a usual night?

acceptedIdeas: A check on how many rows the job wrote compared with a usual night
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A check on how many rows the job wrote compared with a usual night

questions.onCorrect: Only the number of rows is out of line: 600,000 is half the usual 1,200,000, although the job succeeded on time.

misconceptions.feedback: The job reported success, so a check on failure sees nothing wrong.
The job ran in its usual time, so its duration looks normal.

choices.label: A check on how many rows the job wrote compared with a usual night
A check on how long the job took
A check on whether the job failed

questions.prompt: An alert fires when a run writes under 80% of its usual 1,200,000 rows. Below how many rows does it fire?
hints: Convert 80% to a fraction.
The alert fires below this number.
questions.onCorrect: A threshold of this kind adapts to the table's normal size, so a larger table needs a larger count before it alerts.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 20% of the usual rows. The alert fires below 80%.
That is the usual volume. The alert fires below 80% of it.

questions.prompt: A table has grown to 80,000 files of about 100 KB each, and every query on it is slow to start. What is the likely cause?
hints: What does a query have to do for each file before it reads any data?
questions.onCorrect: Each file adds a fixed cost to open, so tens of thousands of tiny files slow every query, and compaction repairs it.

misconceptions.feedback: Skew makes one task run far longer than the others once the work has started. Here the delay is at the start, before any rows are read.
A late source makes the data stale, not the queries slow. These queries are slow every time they run, whatever the data's age.
More cores would open the files faster but would not change the fixed cost of opening, reading the footer of and scheduling each of 80,000 tiny files.

choices.label: Too few cores in the cluster
Data skew, with one key holding most of the rows
A source that delivered late
Too many small files

questions.prompt: How many minutes late is the table, with an age of 385 minutes and a target of 320 minutes?
hints: Subtract the target from the age.
Both are already in minutes.
385 minus 320.
questions.onCorrect: The table's age passes the target by 65 minutes, so the freshness alert should fire.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the age. Subtract the target to find the lateness.
That is the target. The lateness is the age minus the target.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 385 − 320 = 65, so the table is 65 minutes late.

questions.prompt: A job runs at 200,000 rows per second and has 900 million rows to move. How many minutes does it need?
hints: Divide the rows by the rate to get seconds.
Then convert seconds to minutes.
4,500 seconds divided by 60.
questions.onCorrect: Dividing the data by the throughput gives the run time, which can be compared with the deadline.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the time in seconds. The question asks for minutes.
That is the time in hours. The question asks for minutes.

questions.prompt: A table was last loaded at 02:10 and it is now 09:00. Its freshness target is 6 hours. How many minutes late is it?
hints: Work out the age in hours and minutes.
Convert the age and the target to minutes.
Subtract the target.
questions.onCorrect: The age passes the target by 50 minutes, which is the figure an alert would report.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the age in minutes. Subtract the 360-minute target.
That is the target in hours. The question asks for the minutes late.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: From 02:10 to 09:00 is 6 h 50 min, which is 410 minutes. The target is 360 minutes, so it is 50 minutes late.

questions.prompt: A job moves 90,000,000 rows in 30 minutes. How many rows per second is that?
hints: Convert the 30 minutes to seconds.
30 × 60 gives the seconds.
Divide the rows by the seconds.
questions.onCorrect: The rate in rows per second can be set against the rate the deadline requires.

misconceptions.feedback: That is rows per minute. The question asks for rows per second.
That divides by 1,000 seconds. 30 minutes is 1,800 seconds.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 30 minutes is 1,800 seconds, and 90,000,000 ÷ 1,800 = 50,000 rows per second.

questions.prompt: In a shuffle stage, 199 tasks finish in a minute and one runs for twenty minutes. What is the likeliest cause?
hints: Ask why one task in a shuffle would receive far more rows than its siblings.

acceptedIdeas: Data skew, with one key holding most of the rows
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Data skew, with one key holding most of the rows

questions.onCorrect: One task holding far more rows than the rest keeps the stage running after the others have finished.

misconceptions.feedback: Small files slow every task at the start in the same way, so they would not leave one task running twenty times longer than the rest.
Too few cores would make tasks wait in more waves, but each task would still take about the same time. One task taking twenty minutes points to one task with far more data.

choices.label: Too few cores in the cluster
Data skew, with one key holding most of the rows
Too many small files

questions.prompt: Production holds 50,000,000 rows and the test environment runs on a 1% sample. How many rows does test process?
hints: Convert 1% to a fraction.
0.01 times the production rows.
Check that the result is much smaller than production.
questions.onCorrect: A sample keeps the test run cheap and quick while still exercising every step of the pipeline.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 10% of production. A 1% sample is a tenth of that.
That is 0.1% of production. A 1% sample is ten times larger.

questions.prompt: A change has been reviewed and merged to the main branch. Which environment is it deployed to first?
hints: Where does the pipeline run on a sample so that its checks can be made cheaply?
questions.onCorrect: Merging triggers deployment to test, so the change is validated on a sample before it can reach production.

misconceptions.feedback: Development is where the change was made, on a branch, before review. Merging to main is what sends it onward.
Production comes last, once the change has run on a sample of the data and its checks have passed.

choices.label: Development
Production
Test

questions.prompt: A shared table holds 12,000 orders, split equally across 4 regions. A regional manager is allowed to see only the orders of their own region. What should the manager see when they query the table?
hints: The limit is on which orders, that is which rows, the manager may see.

acceptedIdeas: Only the rows for their own region, about a quarter of the table
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only the rows for their own region, about a quarter of the table

questions.onCorrect: The manager sees a quarter of the table, and the other regions' rows are filtered out before the query returns.

misconceptions.feedback: Hiding values in some columns still shows every order, and the manager is not allowed to see other regions' orders at all.
A separate copy for each region is one way to do it, but the same shared table can show each reader only their own rows, with no copy to keep in step.

choices.label: Nothing, until a separate table is made for their region
Only the rows for their own region, about a quarter of the table
All 12,000 rows, with the other regions' amounts hidden

questions.prompt: Support staff may see every customer record but must not see the phone number column. Which control fits?
hints: Is the restriction on some rows or on some columns?
questions.onCorrect: Every row stays visible and only the phone number column is hidden or masked, which is what column-level security does.

misconceptions.feedback: Row-level security decides which rows a person sees. Here the support staff may see every row, and the restriction is on one column.
Read-only access stops a reader from changing the table, but they could still read every phone number.

choices.label: Row-level security
Column-level security
Read-only access

questions.prompt: A password was pasted into a notebook shared with 12 people, and the notebook was also committed to a repository that 30 other people can read. Who can read the password?
hints: Count everyone who can read either copy of the notebook.

acceptedIdeas: All 42 people who can open the notebook or read the repository
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: All 42 people who can open the notebook or read the repository

questions.onCorrect: Each copy of a credential widens the group that holds it, and deleting it from the notebook does not remove it from the history.

misconceptions.feedback: Anyone who can open a notebook can read every line in it, whoever wrote the line.
The repository holds a copy of the notebook, so its 30 readers can read the password as well, and it stays in the repository's history even if it is later deleted.

choices.label: Only the person who pasted it, since it is their notebook
The 12 people the notebook is shared with
All 42 people who can open the notebook or read the repository

questions.prompt: How many parameter values are kept in all, for 3 environments with 4 parameters each?
hints: Each environment has its own set of values.
Multiply the environments by the parameters.
3 times 4.
questions.onCorrect: The table of parameters grows with the environments, while the pipeline code stays the same.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the numbers. Each environment has its own value for every parameter, so they multiply.
That is the parameters of one environment. There are 3 environments.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each of the 3 environments supplies 4 values, so 3 × 4 = 12 values.

questions.prompt: An external auditor must be able to query the monthly revenue table but must not be able to change it. Which kind of access fits?
hints: What is the smallest role that lets the auditor query the table?
questions.onCorrect: Read-only access lets the auditor query the table while the data stays protected against any change.

misconceptions.feedback: An administrator can change and delete anything in the workspace, which is far more than the auditor needs and the opposite of least privilege.
Row-level security decides which rows a reader sees, not whether they can change them. The auditor's need is to read everything and change nothing.

choices.label: Workspace administrator
Read-only access to the table
Row-level security on the table

questions.prompt: A regional manager must see only the rows for their own region in a shared table. Which control fits?
hints: The restriction is on which rows are visible.
Which control filters rows?
questions.onCorrect: Row-level security filters the rows a person can read, so each manager sees only their own region's rows.

misconceptions.feedback: Column-level security hides fields, but the manager here needs only some rows to be hidden.
Masking obscures one column, and all rows would still be visible.
A secret store holds credentials, and it does not restrict which rows a person sees.

choices.label: Row-level security
Masking the email column
Column-level security
A secret store

questions.prompt: Where should the database password used by a pipeline be kept? Give the place, in two words.
hints: It should not be in the notebook or the repository.
A service built to hold credentials.
questions.onCorrect: A secret store holds the credential, the pipeline reads it at run time under its own identity, and it never appears in code.

misconceptions.feedback: Anyone who can read the notebook would then hold the password.

questions.prompt: Which release path follows good practice?
hints: Production should be reached last.
Review and validation come before promotion.
questions.onCorrect: The path runs branch, review, merge and test before production, so every change is reviewed and validated first.

misconceptions.feedback: Editing production first skips review and testing, and leaves no history.
Production would receive the change before it has been validated.
A branch is created before review, since the review is of the branch's changes.

choices.label: Review in test, branch afterwards, then merge
Edit production, then copy the change to test
Branch, review, deploy to test, validate, then promote to production
Merge to main, deploy to production, then validate

acceptedIdeas: Branch, review, deploy to test, validate, then promote to production
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Branch, review, deploy to test, validate, then promote to production

flashcards.front: What does it mean for a pipeline step to be idempotent?
flashcards.back: Running it twice leaves the destination in the same state as running it once, so a retry cannot double the data.

flashcards.front: A pipeline loads raw files into the destination first and transforms them there. Is that ETL or ELT? Give the three letters.
flashcards.back: ELT loads before it transforms, so the raw data is still in the destination afterwards.

flashcards.front: A keyed upsert loads 3 rows into an empty table and is run twice. How many rows does the table hold?
flashcards.back: The second run finds all three keys and replaces those rows, so the table still holds 3 rows.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The second run finds all three keys and replaces those rows, so the table still holds 3 rows.

flashcards.front: A columnar query needs 3 columns of 8 bytes from a table of 50,000,000 rows. How many gigabytes does it read, ignoring compression?
Why can a Parquet reader skip a row group without reading it?
flashcards.back: The footer records the minimum and maximum of each column chunk, and a filter value outside that range cannot be in the group.

flashcards.front: What is the layout called that stores each record's values together?
flashcards.back: A row-oriented layout keeps one record's values together, which suits fetching whole records by key.

flashcards.front: What is the stored value called that tells an incremental load where to start? Give the term.
flashcards.back: The watermark is the largest change time already loaded, taken from the data, so the next run starts from there.

flashcards.front: Why does an upsert make a replayed batch harmless?
flashcards.back: A row whose key already exists is updated with the same values, and no new row is added, so the second run leaves the table unchanged.

flashcards.front: A table has ids 1 and 2. A batch with ids 2 and 3 is upserted twice. How many rows does the table hold?
flashcards.back: Id 2 is updated and id 3 is added once, so the table holds ids 1, 2 and 3.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Id 2 is updated and id 3 is added once, so the table holds ids 1, 2 and 3.

flashcards.front: Which part of a change log entry decides the order in which entries are applied? Give the term.
flashcards.back: The position fixes where an entry falls in the source's sequence of changes, whereas arrival time depends on the network.

flashcards.front: Why can a timestamp query not find a row that was hard-deleted at the source?
flashcards.back: The row is gone and its timestamp went with it, so the query has nothing to return, whereas the log records the delete as an entry.

flashcards.front: An empty table is given 6 inserts of different keys, 3 updates and 1 delete of an existing row. How many rows does it hold at the end?
flashcards.back: Inserts add 6 rows and the delete removes 1, while updates change no count, so 5 rows remain.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Inserts add 6 rows and the delete removes 1, while updates change no count, so 5 rows remain.

flashcards.front: What do we call the longest chain of dependent tasks, which sets the minimum run time?
flashcards.back: The critical path is the longest chain of tasks that must run one after another, so no number of workers can finish sooner.

flashcards.front: Why must a task be idempotent before it is retried automatically?
flashcards.back: A retry runs the task again on the same inputs, so a task that adds rows or changes state would repeat its effect.

flashcards.front: Task A (4 min) feeds B (3 min) and C (7 min), and D (1 min) reads both B and C. What is the minimum run time in minutes?
flashcards.back: The longest chain is A, C, D, which is 4 + 7 + 1 = 12 minutes.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The longest chain is A, C, D, which is 4 + 7 + 1 = 12 minutes.

flashcards.front: Which system checks a row's schema when it is loaded, and refuses rows that do not fit? Give its name.
flashcards.back: A warehouse applies schema-on-write, so a faulty row is refused at load and readers see only valid rows.

flashcards.front: Why do the bronze, silver and gold layers exist, and not just one table?
flashcards.back: Each layer has a different promise to its readers: bronze keeps everything, silver is clean and consistent, and gold is ready to use.

flashcards.front: A gold table has one row per day for each of 5 regions over 20 days. How many rows does it hold?
flashcards.back: Each of the 20 days has a row for each of the 5 regions, so 20 × 5 = 100 rows.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each of the 20 days has a row for each of the 5 regions, so 20 × 5 = 100 rows.

flashcards.front: In a table format, what is stored in a commit file?
flashcards.back: Each commit lists the data files it adds and the files it removes, so replaying commits in order gives the live files at a version.

flashcards.front: What maintenance job physically deletes files that no retained version needs? Give its name.
flashcards.back: Vacuum frees storage by deleting unreferenced files, and it ends time travel for versions that needed them.

flashcards.front: The latest checkpoint is at version 10 and the latest commit is version 12. How many commit files must a reader apply after the checkpoint?
flashcards.back: The checkpoint covers version 10, so the reader applies versions 11 and 12, which is 2 files.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The checkpoint covers version 10, so the reader applies versions 11 and 12, which is 2 files.

flashcards.front: What do we call skipping whole partitions because a filter names the partition column? Give the term.
flashcards.back: Partition pruning opens only the folders whose partition value matches the filter, so the rest are never read.

flashcards.front: Why is partitioning a large table by customer id usually a mistake?
flashcards.back: It creates millions of tiny partitions, and the cost of opening so many small files outweighs the data they hold.

flashcards.front: A 600 GB table has 120 equal partitions, and a query opens 10 of them. How many gigabytes does it read?
flashcards.back: One partition is 600 ÷ 120 = 5 GB, and 10 of them make 50 GB.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One partition is 600 ÷ 120 = 5 GB, and 10 of them make 50 GB.

flashcards.front: What is the movement of rows across the network so that rows with the same key meet called? Give the term.
flashcards.back: A shuffle sends each row to the task that handles its key, so every output partition reads from every input partition.

flashcards.front: Why does one hot key make a whole stage slow, however many machines there are?
flashcards.back: Every row of the key goes to one task, and a stage ends only when its slowest task ends, so extra machines cannot share that task.

flashcards.front: A stage has 60 equal tasks and 16 cores. How many waves does it need?
flashcards.back: 60 ÷ 16 = 3.75, and the partly filled last wave still takes a round, so 4 waves.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 60 ÷ 16 = 3.75, and the partly filled last wave still takes a round, so 4 waves.

flashcards.front: Why does `SELECT DISTINCT` not remove a re-sent record that has a new load time? Answer in a sentence.
flashcards.back: `DISTINCT` compares every column, so a row that differs only in `loaded_at` counts as a different row and survives.

flashcards.front: In SQLite, what does `CAST('x' AS REAL)` return? Give the number.
flashcards.back: SQLite returns 0 without an error, so a bad value quietly counts as zero in a sum unless it is tested first.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: SQLite returns 0 without an error, so a bad value quietly counts as zero in a sum unless it is tested first.

flashcards.front: Which table keeps rows that failed a check, together with the reason they failed? Give its two-word name.
flashcards.back: A reject table preserves the failing rows and their reasons, so failures can be counted and repaired.

flashcards.front: Which time is used to place a record in a window by default in a good stream design: event time or processing time? Give the term.
flashcards.back: Event time puts a record where it happened, so results do not change with network delays.

flashcards.front: Why must a sink tolerate duplicates when the source delivers at-least-once?
flashcards.back: After a failure the consumer restarts at its last committed offset, so records processed since that commit are delivered again.

flashcards.front: The latest event time is 12:30 and the allowed lateness is 5 minutes. What is the watermark? Give it as hh:mm.
flashcards.back: The watermark is the latest event time minus the allowed lateness, so 12:30 minus 5 minutes is 12:25.

flashcards.front: What do we call the action of setting failing rows aside in their own table, with the reason, while the rest continue? Give the term.
flashcards.back: Quarantine keeps the failing rows and their reasons, so they can be counted and repaired.

flashcards.front: Why is silently adapting to any schema change dangerous?
flashcards.back: A bug or a meaning change at the source then flows into every downstream table without anyone noticing it.

flashcards.front: A gate stops a run when more than 5% of rows fail. A batch of 400 rows has 18 failing rows. What percentage fails? Give the number.
flashcards.back: 18 ÷ 400 = 0.045, which is 4.5%, below the 5% limit.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 18 ÷ 400 = 0.045, which is 4.5%, below the 5% limit.

flashcards.front: What do we call the age of the newest data in a table when someone looks at it? Give the term.
flashcards.back: Freshness is measured against the service target, so a table can be late even when every job succeeded.

flashcards.front: Why is it not enough to alert only when a job fails?
flashcards.back: A job can succeed and still write half the usual rows or deliver stale data, so volume, freshness and duration need their own checks.

flashcards.front: A job moves 36 million rows in 10 minutes. How many rows per second is that?
flashcards.back: 10 minutes is 600 seconds, and 36,000,000 ÷ 600 = 60,000 rows per second.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 10 minutes is 600 seconds, and 36,000,000 ÷ 600 = 60,000 rows per second.

flashcards.front: What do we call moving a change from development to test to production? Give the term.
flashcards.back: Promotion carries the same code through each environment in turn, with parameters supplied by each environment.

flashcards.front: Why should a database password not be pasted into a notebook?
flashcards.back: Everyone who can read the notebook, or its history, then holds the credential, and deleting it later does not remove it from the history.

flashcards.front: A pipeline runs in 4 environments and each has 5 parameters. How many parameter values are kept in all?
flashcards.back: Each environment holds its own 5 values, so 4 × 5 = 20 values.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each environment holds its own 5 values, so 4 × 5 = 20 values.
